lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Chemical equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse rates become equal, so concentrations stop changing although both reactions continue.
  • Dynamic equilibrium is established in a closed vessel when the forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until the two rates are equal.
  • Law of mass action says the rate of a reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants, each raised to its coefficient.
  • Equilibrium constant for ammonia synthesis N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 is Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2][H2]^3).
  • Direction of a reaction is predicted by comparing Qc with Kc: Qc less than Kc moves forward, Qc greater than Kc moves backward, Qc equal to Kc is already at equilibrium.
  • Equilibrium is attainable from either side because the same equilibrium state is fixed only by the conditions, whether the reaction starts from reactants or from products.
  • Worked Kc values in this chapter are 24.5 mol/dm^3 for N2O decomposition and 0.02 for HI decomposition.

mcqs.q: What is chemical equilibrium?
options: The state where the forward reaction stops completely
The state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse rates become equal
The state where all reactants are converted into products
The state where the concentration of products becomes zero
mcqs.why: The notes define chemical equilibrium as the state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse rates become equal, so concentrations stop changing although both reactions continue.

mcqs.q: How is dynamic equilibrium established in a closed vessel?
options: The forward rate rises and the reverse rate falls until they are equal
Both rates fall to zero at the same time
The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until the two rates are equal
The reverse rate stays zero while the forward rate slows down
mcqs.why: According to the notes, dynamic equilibrium is established in a closed vessel when the forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until the two rates are equal.

mcqs.q: What does the law of mass action state?
options: The rate of a reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants, each raised to its coefficient
The rate of a reaction is inversely proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants
The rate of a reaction depends only on the temperature of the system
The rate of a reaction is equal to the sum of the concentrations of the products
mcqs.why: The law of mass action says the rate of a reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants, each raised to its coefficient.

mcqs.q: What is the equilibrium constant expression for ammonia synthesis, N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3?
mcqs.why: For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, the notes give Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2][H2]^3): product concentrations on top raised to their coefficients, reactant concentrations below raised to their coefficients.

mcqs.q: If Qc is less than Kc, in which direction does the reaction move?
mcqs.why: The notes state that direction is predicted by comparing Qc with Kc: Qc less than Kc moves forward, Qc greater than Kc moves backward, and Qc equal to Kc is already at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: If Qc is greater than Kc, in which direction does the reaction move?
options: It moves equally in both directions with no net change
mcqs.why: When Qc is greater than Kc there is too much product compared with equilibrium, so according to the notes the reaction moves backward until Qc falls to equal Kc.

mcqs.q: What does it mean when Qc is equal to Kc?
options: The reaction is already at equilibrium
The reaction has gone to completion
mcqs.why: The notes state that when Qc equals Kc, the reaction is already at equilibrium, because the current concentrations are exactly the equilibrium concentrations.

mcqs.q: Why is equilibrium attainable from either side?
options: Because equilibrium concentrations depend on which starting material is used
Because a catalyst fixes the equilibrium state from one side only
Because the reaction can only start from the reactants
Because the same equilibrium state is fixed only by the conditions, whether the reaction starts from reactants or from products
mcqs.why: The notes explain that equilibrium is attainable from either side because the same equilibrium state is fixed only by the conditions, whether the reaction starts from reactants or from products.

mcqs.q: What is the worked Kc value given in this chapter for N2O decomposition?
mcqs.why: The key facts list the worked Kc values in this chapter as 24.5 mol/dm^3 for N2O decomposition and 0.02 for HI decomposition, so the value for N2O decomposition is 24.5 mol/dm^3.

mcqs.q: What is the worked Kc value given in this chapter for HI decomposition?
mcqs.why: The key facts state that the worked Kc values in this chapter are 24.5 mol/dm^3 for N2O decomposition and 0.02 for HI decomposition, so the value for HI decomposition is 0.02.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. What are irreversible reactions? Give a few characteristics of them.
Irreversible reactions are reactions that proceed only in the forward direction and go to completion, so the reactants are fully converted into products. Their characteristics are: they occur in one direction only, they do not attain equilibrium, the products cannot be converted back into reactants under the same conditions, and examples are burning of fuel and rusting of iron.

Q2. Define chemical equilibrium state.
Chemical equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction in which the rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the reverse reaction. At this state the concentrations of reactants and products stop changing with time, although both reactions continue to occur at equal rates.

Q3. Give the characteristics of reversible reaction.
A reversible reaction can proceed in both forward and reverse directions, it does not go to completion, and it can attain a state of dynamic equilibrium. It is represented by a double arrow, and its direction can be changed by changing conditions such as concentration, temperature or pressure.

Q4. How is dynamic equilibrium established?
Dynamic equilibrium is established when a reversible reaction is carried out in a closed vessel. At first the forward reaction is fast and the reverse reaction is slow, but as products build up the reverse rate increases and the forward rate decreases. When the two rates become equal, dynamic equilibrium is established and concentrations remain constant.

Q5. Why at equilibrium state reaction does not stop?
At equilibrium the reaction does not stop because both the forward and reverse reactions continue to take place. They occur at exactly equal rates, so the amount of reactants converted into products in a given time equals the amount of products converted back into reactants. The net change is therefore zero, which is why it is called dynamic equilibrium.

Q6. Why is equilibrium state attainable from either way?
Equilibrium can be reached either by starting with reactants or by starting with products, because the same equilibrium state is determined only by the conditions (temperature and concentrations). Whether the reaction moves forward or backward, the rates adjust until they become equal, giving the same equilibrium concentrations in both cases.

Q7. What is relationship between active mass and rate of reaction?
Active mass means the molar concentration of a substance, in mol/dm^3. According to the law of mass action, the rate of a reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation. Increasing concentration therefore increases the reaction rate.

Q8. Derive equilibrium constant expression for the synthesis of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
The synthesis of ammonia is: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. The rate of the forward reaction is proportional to [N2][H2]^3 and the rate of the reverse reaction is proportional to [NH3]^2. At equilibrium the two rates are equal, so Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2][H2]^3). This is the equilibrium constant expression for ammonia synthesis.

Q9. Write the equilibrium constant expression for the following reactions (reactions printed as figures in the book).
The general method is: write the balanced equation, then Kc = (product concentrations raised to their coefficients) divided by (reactant concentrations raised to their coefficients). For example, for the synthesis of ammonia, N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2][H2]^3). Apply the same rule to each reaction printed in the book, using the coefficients shown in its equation.

Q10. How can direction of a reaction be predicted?
The direction of a reaction is predicted by comparing the reaction quotient Qc with the equilibrium constant Kc. Qc is calculated from the current concentrations in the same form as Kc. If Qc is less than Kc, the reaction moves forward; if Qc is greater than Kc, it moves backward; if Qc equals Kc, the reaction is already at equilibrium.

Q11. How can you know that a reaction has achieved an equilibrium state?
A reaction has reached equilibrium when the concentrations of reactants and products stop changing with time, and when observable properties such as colour, pressure or density become constant. At this point the forward and reverse rates are equal, although both reactions are still occurring.

Q12. What are the characteristics of a reaction that establishes equilibrium state at once?
A reaction that reaches equilibrium at once is usually a fast ionic reaction in solution, such as a neutralization or precipitation reaction, where ions meet and react almost instantly. Such reactions have very high rates in both directions, so the balance between forward and reverse rates is established immediately.

Q13. If reaction quotient Qc of a reaction is more than Kc, what will be the direction of the reaction?
If Qc is greater than Kc, there is too much product (or too little reactant) compared with equilibrium. The reaction will therefore move in the reverse direction, converting products back into reactants, until Qc falls to equal Kc and equilibrium is restored.

Q14. An industry was established based upon a reversible reaction.
It failed to achieve products on commercial level. Can you point out the basic reasons of its failure being a chemist? The failure may be because the equilibrium lies far to the left, so the yield of product is very low, or because the reaction is too slow at the chosen conditions. Other reasons are: unsuitable temperature or pressure, absence of a catalyst, an open system from which a reactant or product escapes, or failure to remove the product continuously to shift the equilibrium forward.

mcqs.q: What are irreversible reactions?
options: Reactions that proceed only in the forward direction and go to completion, so reactants are fully converted into products
Reactions that proceed in both forward and reverse directions
Reactions that attain a state of dynamic equilibrium
Reactions whose products are easily converted back into reactants under the same conditions
mcqs.why: Irreversible reactions proceed only in the forward direction and go to completion, so the reactants are fully converted into products, they do not attain equilibrium, and products cannot be converted back under the same conditions.

mcqs.q: Which pair gives examples of irreversible reactions as stated in the notes?
options: Synthesis of ammonia and decomposition of HI
Decomposition of N2O and formation of NO
Burning of fuel and rusting of iron
mcqs.why: The notes give burning of fuel and rusting of iron as examples of irreversible reactions, which occur in one direction only and do not attain equilibrium.

mcqs.q: Which is a characteristic of a reversible reaction?
options: It occurs in one direction only
It does not go to completion and can attain dynamic equilibrium
mcqs.why: A reversible reaction can proceed in both directions, it does not go to completion, it can attain dynamic equilibrium, it is represented by a double arrow, and its direction can be changed by changing concentration, temperature or pressure.

mcqs.q: At the start of a reversible reaction in a closed vessel, how do the rates compare?
options: The forward reaction is fast and the reverse reaction is slow
The reverse reaction is fast and the forward reaction is slow
Both reactions already have exactly equal rates
mcqs.why: The notes say that at first the forward reaction is fast and the reverse reaction is slow, but as products build up the reverse rate increases and the forward rate decreases until the two rates become equal.

mcqs.q: Why does the reaction not stop at the equilibrium state?
options: Because only the forward reaction continues at equilibrium
Because both forward and reverse reactions continue at exactly equal rates, so the net change is zero
Because all reactants have been used up at equilibrium
Because the vessel is open so new reactants keep entering
mcqs.why: At equilibrium both the forward and reverse reactions continue at exactly equal rates, so the amount converted in a given time in one direction equals the amount converted back, giving zero net change; this is why it is called dynamic equilibrium.

mcqs.q: What does active mass mean?
options: The mass of a substance in grams
The total mass of the reaction mixture
The molar concentration of a substance, in mol/dm^3
The mass of the catalyst used in the reaction
mcqs.why: Active mass means the molar concentration of a substance, in mol/dm^3, and by the law of mass action the rate is directly proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants raised to their coefficients.

mcqs.q: For ammonia synthesis, the rate of the forward reaction is proportional to what?
mcqs.why: For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, the notes state the forward rate is proportional to [N2][H2]^3 and the reverse rate is proportional to [NH3]^2; equating them at equilibrium gives Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2][H2]^3).

mcqs.q: How can the direction of a reaction be predicted?
options: By comparing the reaction quotient Qc with the equilibrium constant Kc
By observing only the colour of the reaction mixture
By measuring only the mass of the catalyst
By checking whether the reaction is exothermic
mcqs.why: Direction is predicted by comparing Qc, calculated from current concentrations in the same form as Kc, with Kc: Qc less than Kc moves forward, Qc greater than Kc moves backward, and Qc equal to Kc is at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: How can you know that a reaction has achieved an equilibrium state?
options: The concentrations keep changing rapidly with time
Observable properties such as colour, pressure or density keep changing
The concentrations stop changing with time and observable properties such as colour, pressure or density become constant
The forward reaction stops and only the reverse reaction continues
mcqs.why: A reaction has reached equilibrium when concentrations of reactants and products stop changing with time and observable properties such as colour, pressure or density become constant, with forward and reverse rates equal.

mcqs.q: What type of reaction establishes an equilibrium state at once?
options: A slow reaction between gases at high pressure
A fast ionic reaction in solution, such as neutralization or precipitation
Rusting of iron in moist air
mcqs.why: The notes say a reaction that reaches equilibrium at once is usually a fast ionic reaction in solution, such as neutralization or precipitation, where ions meet and react almost instantly with very high rates in both directions.

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Describe a reversible reaction with the help of an example and graph.
A reversible reaction is one that can proceed in both directions, for example the synthesis of ammonia: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. On a graph of concentration against time, the reactant concentrations fall and the product concentration rises at first, then all curves become horizontal. The flat parts of the graph show that concentrations have become constant, which is the equilibrium state.

Q2. Write down the macroscopic characteristics of dynamic equilibrium.
The macroscopic characteristics of dynamic equilibrium are: the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, the observable properties such as colour, pressure and density do not change, the reaction can be approached from either direction, it occurs only in a closed system, and a catalyst does not change the equilibrium position but helps to reach it faster.

Q3. State the law of Mass Action and derive the expression for equilibrium constant for a general reaction.
The law of mass action states that the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient. For a general reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, forward rate = kf[A]^a[B]^b and reverse rate = kr[C]^c[D]^d. At equilibrium these rates are equal, so kf/kr = ([C]^c[D]^d)/([A]^a[B]^b) = Kc, the equilibrium constant.

Q4. What is the importance of equilibrium constant?
The equilibrium constant Kc tells the extent of a reaction: a large Kc means the equilibrium lies far to the right and the yield of products is high, while a small Kc means the yield is low. It also predicts the direction of a reaction by comparison with Qc, and helps industries choose conditions (temperature, pressure, concentration) that give the maximum yield of product.

mcqs.q: In a graph of concentration against time for a reversible reaction, what do the flat parts of the curves show?
options: That the reaction has stopped completely
That all reactants have been used up
That concentrations have become constant, which is the equilibrium state
That the temperature of the system is falling
mcqs.why: For ammonia synthesis the reactant concentrations fall and the product concentration rises at first, then all curves become horizontal; the flat parts show concentrations have become constant, which is the equilibrium state.

mcqs.q: Which is a macroscopic characteristic of dynamic equilibrium?
options: Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant
Observable properties such as colour and pressure keep changing
Equilibrium occurs only in an open system
A catalyst changes the equilibrium position
mcqs.why: The macroscopic characteristics include constant concentrations, unchanged colour, pressure and density, approach from either direction, occurrence only in a closed system, and a catalyst that does not change the position but helps reach it faster.

mcqs.q: What is the effect of a catalyst on dynamic equilibrium?
options: It changes the equilibrium position towards the products
It changes the equilibrium position towards the reactants
It prevents equilibrium from being established
It does not change the equilibrium position but helps to reach it faster
mcqs.why: The notes list as a macroscopic characteristic that a catalyst does not change the equilibrium position but helps to reach it faster, because it speeds up both forward and reverse reactions.

mcqs.q: For the general reaction aA + bB <=> cC + dD, what is Kc?
mcqs.why: At equilibrium kf[A]^a[B]^b = kr[C]^c[D]^d, so kf/kr = ([C]^c[D]^d) / ([A]^a[B]^b) = Kc, as derived in the notes for a general reaction.

mcqs.q: For the general reaction aA + bB <=> cC + dD, the forward rate is equal to what?
mcqs.why: The notes give forward rate = kf[A]^a[B]^b and reverse rate = kr[C]^c[D]^d for aA + bB <=> cC + dD; at equilibrium these two rates are equal, which leads to the Kc expression.

mcqs.q: What does a large value of Kc indicate?
options: The equilibrium lies far to the left and the yield of products is low
The equilibrium lies far to the right and the yield of products is high
mcqs.why: The equilibrium constant tells the extent of a reaction: a large Kc means the equilibrium lies far to the right and the yield of products is high, while a small Kc means the yield is low.

mcqs.q: What does a small value of Kc indicate?
options: The yield of products is high
The equilibrium lies far to the right
The yield of products is low
mcqs.why: According to the notes on the importance of Kc, a small Kc means the equilibrium lies towards the left and the yield of products is low, whereas a large Kc gives a high yield.

mcqs.q: Besides telling the extent of a reaction, what else does Kc help to do?
options: It predicts the direction of a reaction by comparison with Qc and helps industries choose conditions for maximum yield
It measures the speed of a reaction directly
It replaces the need for a catalyst in industry
It gives the exact time needed to reach equilibrium
mcqs.why: Kc also predicts the direction of a reaction by comparison with Qc, and helps industries choose conditions of temperature, pressure and concentration that give the maximum yield of product.

mcqs.q: Which reversible reaction is used as the example in the long answer on reversible reactions?
mcqs.why: The long answer describes a reversible reaction using ammonia synthesis, N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, as the example, with reactant concentrations falling and product concentration rising before all curves become horizontal.

mcqs.q: Dynamic equilibrium occurs only in which type of system?
options: A system at very low temperature only
mcqs.why: The macroscopic characteristics state that dynamic equilibrium occurs only in a closed system, can be approached from either direction, and has constant concentrations and unchanged observable properties.

lessons.title: Numericals
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1: Kc for N2O decomposition

For the decomposition of dinitrogen oxide (N2O) into nitrogen and oxygen, the equilibrium concentrations of N2O, N2 and O2 are 1.1, 3.90 and 1.95 mol/dm^3 respectively. Find Kc for this reaction.

(Reaction: 2N2O ⇌ 2N2 + O2)

Step 1: Write the Kc expression: Kc = [N2]^2 x [O2] / [N2O]^2.

Step 2: Substitute: Kc = (3.90)^2 x 1.95 / (1.1)^2 = 15.21 x 1.95 / 1.21.

Step 3: Kc = 29.66 / 1.21 = 24.5.

Final answer: Kc = 24.5 mol/dm^3.

Worked Example 2: Kc for HI decomposition

Hydrogen iodide decomposes to form hydrogen and iodine.

If the equilibrium concentration of HI is 0.078 mol/dm^3, and H2 and I2 are each 0.011 mol/dm^3, calculate the equilibrium constant value for this reversible reaction. (Reaction: 2HI ⇌ H2 + I2)

Step 1: Kc = [H2] x [I2] / [HI]^2.

Step 2: Kc = 0.011 x 0.011 / (0.078)^2 = 0.000121 / 0.006084.

Step 3: Kc = 0.0199, about 0.02.

Final answer: Kc = 0.02 (no units, as the units cancel).

Worked Example 3: NO formed in nitrogen fixation

For the fixation of nitrogen, N2 + O2 ⇌ 2NO, at 1500 K the Kc is 1.1 x 10^-5. If equilibrium concentrations of nitrogen and oxygen are 1.7 x 10^-3 and 6.4 x 10^-3 mol/dm^3 respectively, how much NO is formed?

Step 1: Kc = [NO]^2 / ([N2] x [O2]), so [NO]^2 = Kc x [N2] x [O2].

Step 2: [NO]^2 = 1.1 x 10^-5 x 1.7 x 10^-3 x 6.4 x 10^-3 = 1.197 x 10^-10.

Step 3: [NO] = square root (1.197 x 10^-10) = 1.09 x 10^-5 mol/dm^3.

Final answer: NO formed = 1.09 x 10^-5 mol/dm^3.

Worked Example 4: Ammonia concentration at equilibrium

When nitrogen reacts with hydrogen to form ammonia, the equilibrium mixture contains 0.31 mol/dm^3 of nitrogen and 0.50 mol/dm^3 of hydrogen. If Kc is 0.50 mol^-2 dm^6, what is the equilibrium concentration of ammonia?

(Reaction: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3)

Step 1: Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2] x [H2]^3), so [NH3]^2 = Kc x [N2] x [H2]^3.

Step 2: [NH3]^2 = 0.50 x 0.31 x (0.50)^3 = 0.50 x 0.31 x 0.125 = 0.019375.

Step 3: [NH3] = square root (0.019375) = 0.139 mol/dm^3.

Final answer: Equilibrium concentration of ammonia = 0.139 mol/dm^3.

mcqs.q: For 2N2O <=> 2N2 + O2, equilibrium concentrations are [N2O] = 1.1, [N2] = 3.90 and [O2] = 1.95 mol/dm^3. What is Kc?
What is the correct Kc expression for the decomposition 2N2O <=> 2N2 + O2?
mcqs.why: Working: for 2N2O <=> 2N2 + O2, Kc = [N2]^2 x [O2] / [N2O]^2. Substituting the given values gives Kc = (3.90)^2 x 1.95 / (1.1)^2 = 29.66 / 1.21 = 24.5 mol/dm^3.

mcqs.q: For 2HI <=> H2 + I2, [HI] = 0.078 mol/dm^3 and [H2] = [I2] = 0.011 mol/dm^3. What is Kc?
Why does the Kc for HI decomposition, 2HI <=> H2 + I2, have no units?
options: Because the concentrations are all less than 1 mol/dm^3
Because the temperature was not given
Because the units cancel in the Kc expression
mcqs.why: Working: Kc = [H2] x [I2] / [HI]^2 = 0.011 x 0.011 / (0.078)^2 = 0.000121 / 0.006084 = 0.0199, about 0.02. The notes state this Kc has no units, as the units cancel.

mcqs.q: For N2 + O2 <=> 2NO at 1500 K, Kc = 1.1 x 10^-5, [N2] = 1.7 x 10^-3 and [O2] = 6.4 x 10^-3 mol/dm^3. How much NO is formed?
In the NO formation calculation, what is the value of [NO]^2 before taking the square root?
For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, Kc = 0.50 mol^-2 dm^6, [N2] = 0.31 and [H2] = 0.50 mol/dm^3. What is the equilibrium concentration of ammonia?
In the ammonia equilibrium calculation, what is the value of [NH3]^2 before taking the square root?
In the HI decomposition calculation, what is the value of the denominator (0.078)^2?
In the N2O decomposition calculation, what is the value of the numerator (3.90)^2 x 1.95 before dividing by 1.21?
mcqs.why: Working: Kc = [N2]^2 x [O2] / [N2O]^2 = (3.90)^2 x 1.95 / (1.1)^2. The numerator is 15.21 x 1.95 = 29.66, the denominator is 1.21, and Kc = 29.66 / 1.21 = 24.5 mol/dm^3.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, pH = -log[H+], on a scale from 0 to 14.
  • Pure water has pH 7 at 25 degrees C, because [H+] = 10^-7 mol/dm^3.
  • A solution of pH 1 is 10 times stronger (more acidic) than a solution of pH 2, because the pH scale is logarithmic.
  • Lewis acid and base form a coordinate covalent (dative) bond: the base donates a lone pair to the acid.
  • All alkalies are bases but all bases are not alkalies, because some bases, such as copper oxide, do not dissolve in water.
  • Na2SO4 is a neutral salt while NaHSO4 is an acid salt, because it still has one replaceable hydrogen atom.
  • Solubility rules are: all sodium, potassium, ammonium and nitrate salts are soluble; most sulphates are soluble except barium, lead and calcium sulphates; most carbonates are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium.
  • pH and pOH of 0.2 M H2SO4 are pH = 0.40 and pOH = 13.60, using pH + pOH = 14.

mcqs.q: pH of a solution is defined as:
mcqs.why: The notes define pH as the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, pH = -log[H+], measured on a scale from 0 to 14.

mcqs.q: What is the pH of pure water at 25 degrees C, and why?
mcqs.why: In pure water at 25 degrees C, [H+] = 10^-7 mol/dm^3, so pH = -log(10^-7) = 7, which is why pure water is neutral.

mcqs.q: A solution of pH 1 is how many times stronger (more acidic) than a solution of pH 2?
mcqs.why: The pH scale is logarithmic: pH 1 has [H+] = 10^-1 and pH 2 has [H+] = 10^-2, and 10^-1 / 10^-2 = 10, so the pH 1 solution is 10 times stronger.

mcqs.q: Which bond is formed between a Lewis acid and a Lewis base?
mcqs.why: The notes state that a Lewis acid and base form a coordinate covalent (dative) bond, because the base donates a lone pair of electrons to the acid.

mcqs.q: Why are all bases not alkalies, although all alkalies are bases?
options: Because alkalies do not neutralize acids
Because some bases, such as copper oxide, do not dissolve in water
Because bases never give hydroxide ions
Because alkalies are not bases at all
mcqs.why: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Some bases, such as copper oxide, do not dissolve in water, so they are bases but not alkalies, while every alkali is a base.

mcqs.q: Why is NaHSO4 an acid salt while Na2SO4 is a neutral salt?
options: Because NaHSO4 contains sodium but Na2SO4 does not
Because NaHSO4 is insoluble in water
Because NaHSO4 still has one replaceable hydrogen atom
Because Na2SO4 still has one replaceable hydrogen atom
mcqs.why: In Na2SO4 both hydrogen atoms of sulphuric acid are replaced by sodium, leaving none replaceable. In NaHSO4 only one is replaced, so one replaceable hydrogen remains and it is an acid salt.

mcqs.q: Which of the following sulphates is insoluble in water?
mcqs.why: The solubility rules in the notes say most sulphates are soluble, except barium, lead and calcium sulphates, so barium sulphate is the insoluble one here.

mcqs.q: Which of the following carbonates is soluble in water?
mcqs.why: The notes state that most carbonates are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium, so sodium carbonate is soluble while the others listed are not.

mcqs.q: What are the pH and pOH of 0.2 M H2SO4?
mcqs.why: H2SO4 gives two protons, so [H+] = 2 x 0.2 = 0.4 mol/dm^3. pH = -log(0.4) = 0.40, and pOH = 14 - pH = 14 - 0.40 = 13.60.

mcqs.q: The pH scale used to measure acidity or basicity of a solution runs from:
mcqs.why: The notes state that pH = -log[H+] measures how acidic or basic a solution is on a scale from 0 to 14, with 7 as the neutral point.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Name three common household substances having (a) pH greater than 7 (b) pH less than 7 (c) pH equal to 7.
(a) pH greater than 7: soap solution, washing soda solution, and baking soda solution. (b) pH less than 7: vinegar, lemon juice, and tomato juice. (c) pH equal to 7: pure water, common salt solution, and sugar solution.

Q2. Define a base and explain that all alkalies are bases, but all bases are not alkalies.
A base is a substance that neutralizes an acid to form a salt and water, and accepts protons or donates hydroxide ions. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to give hydroxide ions. All alkalies are bases because they neutralize acids, but all bases are not alkalies because some bases, such as copper oxide or calcium carbonate, do not dissolve in water and so are not alkalies.

Q3. Define Bronsted-Lowry base and explain with an example that water is a Bronsted-Lowry base.
A Bronsted-Lowry base is a substance that accepts a proton (H+ ion) from an acid. Water acts as a Bronsted-Lowry base when it reacts with hydrogen chloride: HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl-. Here water accepts a proton from HCl to form the hydronium ion, so water behaves as a base.

Q4. How can you justify that Bronsted-Lowry concept of acid and base is applicable to non-aqueous solutions?
The Bronsted-Lowry concept is based on proton transfer, not on water or hydroxide ions, so it works in any solvent where proton transfer can occur. For example, in liquid ammonia, ammonium chloride acts as an acid by donating a proton and amide ion acts as a base by accepting it, even though no water is present.

Q5. Which kind of bond is formed between Lewis acid and a base?
A coordinate covalent bond (dative bond) is formed between a Lewis acid and a Lewis base. The base donates a lone pair of electrons to the acid, which accepts it into a vacant orbital, and the shared pair forms the bond between them.

Q6. Why does H+ ion act as a Lewis acid?
A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor. The H+ ion has no electrons and has a vacant orbital, so it readily accepts a lone pair of electrons from a base, for example from water to form H3O+. It therefore behaves as a Lewis acid.

Q7. Name two acids used in the manufacture of fertilizers.
Two acids used in fertilizer manufacture are sulphuric acid, used to make ammonium sulphate and superphosphate, and nitric acid, used to make ammonium nitrate and calcium ammonium nitrate.

Q8. Define pH.
What is the pH of pure water? pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, pH = -log[H+]. It measures how acidic or basic a solution is on a scale from 0 to 14. The pH of pure water at 25 degrees C is 7, because [H+] = 10^-7 mol/dm^3, so water is neutral.

Q9. How many times a solution of pH 1 will be stronger than that of a solution having pH 2?
The pH scale is logarithmic, so each whole unit of pH means a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration. A solution of pH 1 has [H+] = 10^-1, while pH 2 has [H+] = 10^-2. The pH 1 solution is therefore 10 times stronger (more acidic) than the pH 2 solution.

Q10. Define the following: (i) Normal salt (ii) Basic salt.
(i) A normal salt is formed when all the replaceable hydrogen atoms of an acid are replaced by a metal or ammonium ion, for example NaCl and Na2SO4. (ii) A basic salt is formed when only some of the hydroxide ions of a base are replaced by an acid radical, so it still contains a hydroxide group, for example Pb(OH)NO3 and Mg(OH)Cl.

Q11. Na2SO4 is a neutral salt while NaHSO4 is an acid salt.
Justify. Na2SO4 is formed when both hydrogen atoms of sulphuric acid are replaced by sodium, so it has no replaceable hydrogen left and its solution is neutral. NaHSO4 is formed when only one hydrogen atom is replaced, leaving one acidic hydrogen (HSO4-) that can still be donated, so it behaves as an acid salt.

Q12. Give a few characteristic properties of salts.
Salts are generally crystalline solids with high melting points, they are formed by neutralization of acids and bases, many dissolve in water to give neutral, acidic or basic solutions, they conduct electricity when molten or in solution, and they have characteristic colours and tastes (for example copper sulphate is blue).

Q13. How are the soluble salts recovered from water?
Soluble salts are recovered from water by evaporation or crystallization. The salt solution is heated gently to evaporate the water, or it is concentrated and then cooled so that pure crystals of the salt separate out, which are then filtered and dried.

Q14. How are the insoluble salts prepared?
Insoluble salts are prepared by precipitation: two soluble salt solutions are mixed so that the insoluble salt forms as a solid precipitate. The precipitate is then filtered off, washed with distilled water to remove soluble impurities, and dried.

Q15. Why is a salt neutral? Explain with an example.
A salt is neutral when it is formed from a strong acid and a strong base, because neither of its ions reacts with water to produce excess H+ or OH- ions. For example, sodium chloride is formed from strong acid HCl and strong base NaOH, so its solution has pH 7 and is neutral.

Q16. Name an acid used in the preservation of food.
Acetic acid (vinegar) is used in the preservation of food, for example in pickles and sauces. Citric acid is also used to preserve jams, squashes and soft drinks.

Q17. Name the acids present in: (i) Vinegar (ii) Ant sting (iii) Citrus fruit (iv) Sour milk.
(i) Vinegar: acetic acid. (iii) Citrus fruit: citric acid. (iv) Sour milk: lactic acid.

Q18. How can you justify that Pb(OH)NO3 is a basic salt?
Pb(OH)NO3 still contains a hydroxide (OH) group from the base Pb(OH)2, because only one of the two hydroxide groups has been replaced by the nitrate group. Since it contains both a basic hydroxide part and an acid radical, it is a basic salt.

Q19. You are in a need of an acidic salt. How can you prepare it?
An acidic salt is prepared by partially neutralizing a polybasic acid with a base, using less base than needed for full neutralization. For example, adding a limited amount of NaOH to sulphuric acid gives sodium hydrogen sulphate (NaHSO4), an acidic salt that still contains a replaceable hydrogen atom.

Q20. Which salt is used to prepare plaster of Paris?
Calcium sulphate dihydrate (gypsum, CaSO4.2H2O) is heated to about 120 degrees C to remove part of its water of crystallization, giving calcium sulphate hemihydrate (CaSO4.1/2H2O), which is plaster of Paris.

mcqs.q: Which of the following household substances has a pH greater than 7?
mcqs.why: The notes list soap solution, washing soda solution and baking soda solution as household substances with pH greater than 7, while vinegar, lemon juice and tomato juice have pH less than 7.

mcqs.q: An alkali is best defined as a base that:
options: Dissolves in water to give hydroxide ions
Donates a proton to an acid
mcqs.why: The notes define an alkali as a base that dissolves in water to give hydroxide ions. All alkalies are bases because they neutralize acids, but insoluble bases are not alkalies.

mcqs.q: In the reaction HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl-, water acts as a Bronsted-Lowry base because it:
options: Accepts a proton from HCl to form the hydronium ion
Donates a hydroxide ion to HCl
Accepts an electron pair from HCl
mcqs.why: A Bronsted-Lowry base accepts a proton (H+ ion). Here water accepts a proton from HCl to form H3O+, so water behaves as a Bronsted-Lowry base in this reaction.

mcqs.q: Why is the Bronsted-Lowry concept applicable to non-aqueous solutions?
options: Because it is based on hydroxide ions in water
Because it requires water as the solvent
Because it only works for strong acids
Because it is based on proton transfer, not on water or hydroxide ions
mcqs.why: The concept rests on proton transfer, so it works in any solvent where protons can be transferred; for example in liquid ammonia, ammonium chloride acts as an acid and the amide ion as a base, with no water present.

mcqs.q: Why does the H+ ion act as a Lewis acid?
options: Because it donates a lone pair of electrons
Because it has many electrons to share
Because it has no electrons and a vacant orbital, so it accepts a lone pair
Because it always forms ionic bonds
mcqs.why: A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor. The H+ ion has no electrons and has a vacant orbital, so it readily accepts a lone pair from a base, for example from water to form H3O+.

mcqs.q: Which pair of acids is used in the manufacture of fertilizers?
mcqs.why: The notes name sulphuric acid, used to make ammonium sulphate and superphosphate, and nitric acid, used to make ammonium nitrate and calcium ammonium nitrate, as acids used in fertilizer manufacture.

mcqs.q: A normal salt is one in which:
options: Only some hydrogen atoms of the acid are replaced
A hydroxide group still remains in the salt
All the replaceable hydrogen atoms of an acid are replaced by a metal or ammonium ion
mcqs.why: The notes define a normal salt as formed when all the replaceable hydrogen atoms of an acid are replaced by a metal or ammonium ion, for example NaCl and Na2SO4.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a basic salt?
mcqs.why: A basic salt still contains a hydroxide group because only some hydroxide ions of the base were replaced. Pb(OH)NO3 (and Mg(OH)Cl) are the examples given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Insoluble salts are prepared by the method of:
options: Filtration of a metal from an acid
mcqs.why: The notes state that insoluble salts are prepared by precipitation: two soluble salt solutions are mixed so the insoluble salt forms as a solid precipitate, which is then filtered, washed and dried.

mcqs.q: Plaster of Paris is prepared by heating which salt to about 120 degrees C?
mcqs.why: Gypsum, CaSO4.2H2O, is heated to about 120 degrees C to remove part of its water of crystallization, giving calcium sulphate hemihydrate (CaSO4.1/2H2O), which is plaster of Paris.

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Define an acid and a base according to Bronsted-Lowry concept and justify with examples that water is an amphoteric compound.
According to Bronsted-Lowry, an acid donates a proton and a base accepts a proton. Water is amphoteric because it can do both: with HCl it accepts a proton (HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl-) and acts as a base, while with ammonia it donates a proton (NH3 + H2O → NH4+ + OH-) and acts as an acid. Water can therefore behave as either an acid or a base depending on the other substance.

Q2. Explain the Lewis concept of acids and bases.
According to Lewis, an acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a base is an electron-pair donor. When a base donates a lone pair to an acid, a coordinate covalent bond forms. For example, ammonia (base) donates its lone pair to boron trifluoride (acid) to form NH3.BF3. This concept is wider than earlier ones because it also covers reactions with no protons or hydrogen ions.

Q3. What is auto-ionization of water? How is it used to establish the pH of water?
Auto-ionization (self-ionization) of water is the reaction in which two water molecules transfer a proton between themselves: 2H2O ⇌ H3O+ + OH-. At 25 degrees C the product [H+][OH-] = 10^-14, and since [H+] = [OH-] in pure water, [H+] = 10^-7 mol/dm^3. Therefore pH = -log(10^-7) = 7, establishing that pure water is neutral.

Q4. Define a salt and give the characteristic properties of salts.
A salt is an ionic compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion, usually by neutralization of an acid with a base. Its properties are: it is a crystalline solid, it has a high melting point, it is often soluble in water, its solution or melt conducts electricity, and it may be neutral, acidic or basic depending on the strength of the acid and base from which it came.

Q5. Explain with examples how soluble salts are prepared.
Soluble salts are prepared by: (i) neutralization of an acid with a base, for example HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O; (ii) reaction of an acid with a metal, for example 2HCl + Zn → ZnCl2 + H2; (iii) reaction of an acid with a metal oxide or carbonate, for example 2HCl + CaCO3 → CaCl2 + CO2 + H2O. The salt is then recovered by evaporation or crystallization.

Q6. Give the characteristics of an acidic salt.
An acidic salt still contains one or more replaceable hydrogen atoms, so its solution is acidic (pH less than 7). It is formed by partial neutralization of a polybasic acid, for example NaHSO4 and NaHCO3. On heating or on reaction with a base it can lose its remaining hydrogen and change into a normal salt.

Q7. Give four uses of calcium oxide.
Four uses of calcium oxide (quicklime) are: in the manufacture of cement and mortar; to neutralize acidic soils in agriculture; in the purification of sugar and in water treatment to remove hardness; and in the manufacture of bleaching powder and glass.

Q8. You are having a strong acid (HNO3) and strong base (NaOH) on mixing: (i) What type of salt will you have? (ii) What type of reaction will it be? (iii) Will it be soluble or insoluble salt? (iv) If it is soluble, how will it be recovered?
(i) A normal, neutral salt, sodium nitrate (NaNO3). (ii) A neutralization reaction: HNO3 + NaOH → NaNO3 + H2O. (iii) It will be a soluble salt, as all nitrates and sodium salts are soluble. (iv) It is recovered by evaporating the water, or by concentrating the solution and cooling it so that crystals of sodium nitrate separate, which are then filtered and dried.

Q9. Explain why: (i) HCl forms only one series of salts. (ii) H2SO4 forms two series of salts. (iii) H3PO4 forms three series of salts. Give necessary equations.
The number of series of salts equals the number of replaceable hydrogen atoms in the acid. (i) HCl is monobasic with one hydrogen: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O, giving only one series. (ii) H2SO4 is dibasic: partial neutralization gives NaHSO4, full neutralization gives Na2SO4, giving two series. (iii) H3PO4 is tribasic: it gives NaH2PO4, Na2HPO4 and Na3PO4, giving three series of salts.

Q10. Classify the following salts as soluble or insoluble salts: (i) Sodium chloride (ii) Silver nitrate (iii) Lead chloride (iv) Copper sulphate (v) Barium sulphate (vi) Ammonium chloride (vii) Sodium carbonate (viii) Calcium carbonate (ix) Ferric chloride (x) Magnesium sulphate.
Soluble: sodium chloride, silver nitrate, copper sulphate, ammonium chloride, sodium carbonate, ferric chloride, magnesium sulphate. Insoluble (or sparingly soluble): lead chloride (soluble only in hot water), barium sulphate, calcium carbonate. The general rules are: all sodium, potassium, ammonium and nitrate salts are soluble; most sulphates are soluble except barium, lead and calcium sulphates; most carbonates are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium.

Q11. Complete and balance the following equations (equations printed as figures in the book).
Balance each equation by making the number of atoms of every element equal on both sides, following the method: write the unbalanced equation, count atoms on each side, adjust coefficients starting with the most complex compound, and check that all atoms and charges balance. Apply this to each equation printed in the book, keeping the reactants and products exactly as shown there.

mcqs.q: Water is amphoteric. In the reaction NH3 + H2O -> NH4+ + OH-, water acts as:
options: A base, because it accepts a proton
An acid, because it donates a proton
A salt, because it neutralizes ammonia
An alkali, because it dissolves in water
mcqs.why: According to Bronsted-Lowry, an acid donates a proton. With ammonia, water donates a proton to form NH4+ and OH-, so water acts as an acid; with HCl it accepts a proton, which makes water amphoteric.

mcqs.q: According to the Lewis concept, when ammonia reacts with boron trifluoride to form NH3.BF3:
options: Ammonia is the acid and BF3 is the base
Ammonia is the base donating a lone pair and BF3 is the acid accepting it
mcqs.why: Lewis defines an acid as an electron-pair acceptor and a base as an electron-pair donor. Ammonia donates its lone pair to boron trifluoride, forming a coordinate covalent bond in NH3.BF3.

mcqs.q: The auto-ionization (self-ionization) of water is represented by:
mcqs.why: The notes describe auto-ionization as two water molecules transferring a proton between themselves: 2H2O <=> H3O+ + OH-, producing hydronium and hydroxide ions in equal amounts.

mcqs.q: Using auto-ionization, the pH of pure water at 25 degrees C is established as 7 because:
mcqs.why: At 25 degrees C, [H+][OH-] = 10^-14 and in pure water [H+] = [OH-], so [H+] = square root of 10^-14 = 10^-7 mol/dm^3. Then pH = -log(10^-7) = 7, showing pure water is neutral.

mcqs.q: Which reaction shows the preparation of a soluble salt from an acid and a metal?
mcqs.why: The notes give reaction of an acid with a metal as one method for soluble salts: 2HCl + Zn -> ZnCl2 + H2. The other options show neutralization, reaction with a carbonate, and ionization in water.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes an acidic salt?
options: Its solution has pH greater than 7
It is formed by complete neutralization of a monobasic acid
It still contains a hydroxide group
It still contains one or more replaceable hydrogen atoms, so its solution is acidic (pH less than 7)
mcqs.why: The notes state that an acidic salt still contains replaceable hydrogen atoms and is formed by partial neutralization of a polybasic acid, for example NaHSO4 and NaHCO3, so its solution has pH less than 7.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a use of calcium oxide (quicklime)?
options: To neutralize acidic soils in agriculture
To make ammonium nitrate fertilizer directly
mcqs.why: The notes list four uses of calcium oxide: making cement and mortar, neutralizing acidic soils in agriculture, purification of sugar and water treatment, and manufacture of bleaching powder and glass.

mcqs.q: On mixing strong acid HNO3 with strong base NaOH, the salt formed is:
options: An insoluble basic salt, lead nitrate
A normal, neutral soluble salt, sodium nitrate (NaNO3)
No salt is formed in this reaction
mcqs.why: The reaction HNO3 + NaOH -> NaNO3 + H2O is a neutralization giving a normal, neutral salt. Sodium nitrate is soluble because all nitrates and all sodium salts are soluble, and it is recovered by evaporation or crystallization.

mcqs.q: H3PO4 forms three series of salts because it:
options: Is a strong acid with no replaceable hydrogen
Has three replaceable hydrogen atoms, giving NaH2PO4, Na2HPO4 and Na3PO4
Reacts with three different metals only
mcqs.why: The number of series of salts equals the number of replaceable hydrogen atoms. H3PO4 is tribasic with three replaceable hydrogens, so it gives NaH2PO4, Na2HPO4 and Na3PO4: three series.

mcqs.q: Based on the solubility rules in the notes, which salt is insoluble?
mcqs.why: All sodium, potassium, ammonium and nitrate salts are soluble, and most sulphates are soluble except barium, lead and calcium sulphates. Hence barium sulphate is insoluble, while the other three listed are soluble.

lessons.title: Numericals
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example 1: pH and pOH of 0.2 M H2SO4

Calculate the pH and pOH of 0.2 M H2SO4.

Step 1: Sulphuric acid gives two protons; taking both into account, [H+] = 2 x 0.2 = 0.4 mol/dm^3.

Step 2: pH = -log(0.4) = 0.40.

Step 3: pOH = 14 - pH = 14 - 0.40 = 13.60.

Final answer: pH = 0.40, pOH = 13.60 (for the first proton only, pH = 0.70).

Worked Example 2: pH of 0.1 M KOH

Calculate the pH of 0.1 M KOH.

Step 1: [OH-] = 0.1 mol/dm^3.

Step 2: pOH = -log(0.1) = 1.

Step 3: pH = 14 - pOH = 14 - 1 = 13.

Final answer: pH = 13.

Worked Example 3: pOH of 0.004 M HNO3

Calculate the pOH of 0.004 M HNO3.

Step 1: [H+] = 0.004 mol/dm^3.

Step 2: pH = -log(0.004) = 2.40.

Step 3: pOH = 14 - 2.40 = 11.60.

Final answer: pOH = 11.60.

Worked Example 4: pH and pOH table for seven solutions

Complete the following table: (i) 0.15 M HI (ii) 0.040 M KOH (iii) 0.020 M Ba(OH)2 (iv) 0.00030 M HClO4 (v) 0.55 M NaOH (vi) 0.055 M HCl (vii) 0.055 M Ca(OH)2. Give [H+], [OH-], pH and pOH for each.

Step 1: (i) 0.15 M HI: [H+] = 0.15, pH = 0.82, pOH = 13.18, [OH-] = 6.6 x 10^-14.

Step 2: (ii) 0.040 M KOH: [OH-] = 0.040, pOH = 1.40, pH = 12.60, [H+] = 2.5 x 10^-13.

Step 3: (iii) 0.020 M Ba(OH)2: [OH-] = 0.040, pOH = 1.40, pH = 12.60, [H+] = 2.5 x 10^-13.

Step 4: (iv) 0.00030 M HClO4: [H+] = 3.0 x 10^-4, pH = 3.52, pOH = 10.48, [OH-] = 3.3 x 10^-11.

Step 5: (v) 0.55 M NaOH: [OH-] = 0.55, pOH = 0.26, pH = 13.74, [H+] = 1.8 x 10^-14.

Step 6: (vi) 0.055 M HCl: [H+] = 0.055, pH = 1.26, pOH = 12.74, [OH-] = 1.8 x 10^-13.

Step 7: (vii) 0.055 M Ca(OH)2: [OH-] = 0.11, pOH = 0.96, pH = 13.04, [H+] = 9.1 x 10^-14.

Final answer: Table as above, using pH + pOH = 14 and [H+][OH-] = 10^-14.

mcqs.q: Calculate the pH of 0.2 M H2SO4, taking both protons into account.
mcqs.why: H2SO4 gives two protons, so [H+] = 2 x 0.2 = 0.4 mol/dm^3. pH = -log[H+] = -log(0.4) = 0.40.

mcqs.q: Calculate the pH of 0.1 M KOH.
mcqs.why: KOH gives [OH-] = 0.1 mol/dm^3. pOH = -log[OH-] = -log(0.1) = 1. pH = 14 - pOH = 14 - 1 = 13.

mcqs.q: Calculate the pOH of 0.004 M HNO3.
Calculate the pH of 0.15 M HI.
Calculate the pH of 0.020 M Ba(OH)2.
Calculate the pH of 0.00030 M HClO4.
Calculate the pOH of 0.55 M NaOH.
mcqs.why: NaOH gives [OH-] = 0.55 mol/dm^3. pOH = -log[OH-] = -log(0.55) = 0.26 (and pH = 14 - 0.26 = 13.74).

mcqs.q: Calculate the pH of 0.055 M HCl.
Calculate the pH of 0.055 M Ca(OH)2.
mcqs.why: Ca(OH)2 gives two OH- ions, so [OH-] = 2 x 0.055 = 0.11 mol/dm^3. pOH = -log(0.11) = 0.96. pH = 14 - 0.96 = 13.04.

mcqs.q: Calculate the pOH of 0.2 M H2SO4, taking both protons into account.
mcqs.why: H2SO4 gives two protons, so [H+] = 2 x 0.2 = 0.4 mol/dm^3. pH = -log(0.4) = 0.40. pOH = 14 - pH = 14 - 0.40 = 13.60.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Catenation is the ability of an element to link with atoms of itself to form long chains or rings; carbon shows it most strongly.
  • Coal types by carbon content are peat (about 60%), lignite (about 70%), bituminous coal (about 80%) and anthracite (about 90%).
  • Functional group is an atom or group of atoms that gives an organic compound its characteristic properties and reactions, for example -OH in alcohols.
  • Homologous series is a family with the same functional group and general formula, differing by a -CH2- group between successive members, for example alkanes CnH2n+2.
  • Organic compounds are numerous because carbon catenates into chains, branches and rings, forms four strong covalent bonds, and shows isomerism.
  • Amines contain the -NH2 group: primary amines have one alkyl group, secondary two, tertiary three.
  • Alkenes and alkynes are identified by decolourizing bromine water and dilute KMnO4 solution, which alkanes do not.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. What is meant by the term catenation? Give an example of a compound that displays catenation.
Catenation is the ability of an element to link with atoms of itself to form long chains or rings. Carbon shows catenation most strongly: for example, in butane (C4H10) four carbon atoms link together in a chain, and in benzene six carbon atoms link in a ring.

Q2. How is coal formed?
Coal is formed from dead plants buried under layers of earth millions of years ago. Under high pressure and temperature, and without air, the plant material slowly lost oxygen and hydrogen and became richer in carbon, passing through the stages of peat, lignite, bituminous coal and anthracite.

Q3. What is the importance of natural gas?
Natural gas is important as a clean fuel for cooking, heating, electricity generation and vehicles, and as a raw material for making fertilizers, plastics and other chemicals. It burns with a blue flame, produces less smoke than coal or oil, and is mainly methane.

Q4. Justify that organic compounds are used as food.
Organic compounds are used as food because our bodies need carbohydrates, proteins, fats and vitamins, all of which are organic compounds. Carbohydrates and fats give energy, proteins build and repair body tissues, and vitamins regulate body functions, so food is essentially a mixture of organic compounds.

Q5. How are alkyl radicals formed? Explain with examples.
Alkyl radicals are formed when one hydrogen atom is removed from an alkane molecule. For example, removing one hydrogen from methane (CH4) gives the methyl radical (CH3-), and removing one from ethane (C2H6) gives the ethyl radical (C2H5-). They are represented by R- and are very reactive.

Q6. What is the difference between n-propyl and isopropyl radicals? Explain with structure.
n-Propyl (CH3-CH2-CH2-) is formed by removing a hydrogen from the end carbon of propane, so the free valency is on a primary carbon. Isopropyl (CH3-CH(-)-CH3) is formed by removing a hydrogen from the middle carbon, so the free valency is on a secondary carbon. They have the same formula C3H7 but different structures.

Q7. Explain different radicals of butane.
Butane (C4H10) gives two radicals: n-butyl (CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-) by removing a hydrogen from an end carbon, and sec-butyl (CH3-CH2-CH(-)-CH3) by removing a hydrogen from a middle carbon. The two radicals differ in the position of the free valency and in their properties.

Q8. Define functional group with an example.
A functional group is an atom or a group of atoms that gives an organic compound its characteristic properties and reactions. For example, the hydroxyl group (-OH) is the functional group of alcohols: ethanol (C2H5OH) behaves as an alcohol because of its -OH group.

Q9. What is an ester group? Write down the formula of ethyl acetate.
An ester group is -COO-, formed when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid. Esters have sweet, fruity smells and are used as flavours and solvents. Ethyl acetate is CH3COOC2H5, formed from acetic acid and ethanol.

Q10. Write down the dot and cross formulae of propane and n-butane.
Propane (C3H8): three carbon atoms in a chain, each carbon sharing electron pairs with hydrogen atoms and neighbouring carbons, giving 8 hydrogens in total (CH3-CH2-CH3). n-Butane (C4H10): four carbon atoms in a straight chain with 10 hydrogens (CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3). In dot-and-cross diagrams, draw each shared pair as one dot from one atom and one cross from the other.

Q11. Define structural formula. Draw the structural formulae of n-butane and isobutane.
A structural formula shows how the atoms in a molecule are arranged and bonded to each other. n-Butane is CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3, a straight chain of four carbons. Isobutane is CH3-CH(-CH3)-CH3, a branched chain in which the middle carbon carries an extra methyl group.

Q12. Write classification of coal.
Coal is classified into four types by carbon content: peat (about 60% carbon, soft and brown), lignite (about 70% carbon), bituminous coal (about 80% carbon, the common coal used for fuel), and anthracite (about 90% carbon, hard, shiny and the best quality coal).

Q13. What are heterocyclic compounds? Give two examples.
Heterocyclic compounds are ring compounds in which the ring contains atoms other than carbon, such as nitrogen, oxygen or sulphur. Two examples are pyridine (a six-membered ring with one nitrogen atom) and furan (a five-membered ring with one oxygen atom).

Q14. Why are benzene and other homologous compounds of benzene called aromatic compounds?
Benzene and its homologues are called aromatic because they were first obtained from fragrant (aromatic) plant products such as balsams and resins, and because they share a special ring structure with delocalized electrons. They undergo substitution reactions rather than addition reactions, which is characteristic of aromatic compounds.

lessons.notes_html:
Q1. (a) How is coal formed? What are the different types of coal? (b) Write down the composition and uses of different types of coal.
(a) Coal formed from dead plants buried under earth over millions of years, under pressure and heat without air, changing from peat to lignite to bituminous coal to anthracite. (b) Peat (60% carbon) is used as a poor fuel; lignite (70%) is used in power stations; bituminous coal (80%) is the main fuel for industry and for making coke; anthracite (90%) is the cleanest, hardest coal, used for domestic heating and in metallurgy.

Q2. (a) What is destructive distillation of coal? (b) Name the different types of products obtained by the destructive distillation of coal.
(a) Destructive distillation of coal is heating coal strongly in the absence of air, so it decomposes instead of burning. (b) Its products are: coal gas (used as fuel), ammoniacal liquor (used to make fertilizers), coal tar (used for roads, dyes and medicines), and coke (a nearly pure carbon residue used as fuel and in iron extraction).

Q3. Write a detailed note on functional groups of alkenes and alkynes. How are they identified from other compounds?
The functional group of alkenes is the carbon-carbon double bond (C=C), and of alkynes it is the carbon-carbon triple bond (C≡C). They are identified by their addition reactions: both decolourize bromine water and dilute KMnO4 solution, which alkanes do not. Alkynes are also identified by their reaction with ammoniacal silver nitrate, which gives a white precipitate with terminal alkynes.

Q4. Give some uses of organic compounds in our daily life.
Organic compounds are used as food (carbohydrates, proteins, fats), clothing (cotton, wool, nylon), fuel (petrol, natural gas, kerosene), medicines (aspirin, antibiotics), soaps and detergents, plastics, paints, dyes, perfumes, and in the manufacture of paper, rubber and fertilizers.

Q5. Write down the characteristics of homologous series.
A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, differing by a -CH2- group between successive members. Its characteristics are: all members have similar chemical properties, physical properties change gradually with molecular mass, all can be made by similar methods, and they have the same general formula, for example alkanes CnH2n+2.

Q6. Why are organic compounds numerous?
Organic compounds are numerous because carbon shows catenation, forming long chains, branches and rings of almost any length, and because carbon forms four strong covalent bonds, allowing many combinations with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and halogens. Isomerism also multiplies the number: the same formula can give many different structures.

Q7. What are amines? Explain the different types of amines giving an example of each type. How is primary amino group identified?
Amines are organic compounds containing the amino group -NH2, derived from ammonia by replacing hydrogen atoms with alkyl groups. Primary amines have one alkyl group (methylamine, CH3NH2), secondary amines have two (dimethylamine), and tertiary amines have three (trimethylamine). A primary amino group is identified by the carbylamine test: warming with chloroform and alcoholic KOH gives a foul-smelling isocyanide.

Q8. Describe the functional group of an alcohol. How are alcoholic groups identified?
The functional group of an alcohol is the hydroxyl group -OH attached to a carbon atom. Alcohols are identified by their reaction with sodium metal, which gives hydrogen gas, and by the formation of a sweet-smelling ester when warmed with a carboxylic acid and concentrated sulphuric acid. Ethanol also gives a characteristic smell and burns with a blue flame.

Q9. Differentiate between aldehydic and ketonic functional groups. How are both identified from each other?
The aldehydic group is -CHO, at the end of a carbon chain, while the ketonic group is >C=O, in the middle of a chain with two carbon groups attached. Aldehydes are identified by Tollens' test (silver mirror with ammoniacal silver nitrate) and Fehling's test (red precipitate), which ketones do not give, because aldehydes are easily oxidized while ketones are not.

Q10. Encircle the functional groups in the following compounds (compounds printed as figures in the book). Also give the names of the functional groups.
Identify each compound printed in the book and mark the atom or group that gives it its character: -OH is hydroxyl (alcohol), -CHO is aldehydic, >C=O is ketonic, -COOH is carboxylic acid, -COO- is ester, -NH2 is amino, and -X is halo group. Name the group found in each printed compound by matching it with this list.

Q11. What are the general properties of organic compounds?
Organic compounds are usually covalent, so they have low melting and boiling points, are often insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents, do not conduct electricity, burn in air to give carbon dioxide and water, and react slowly compared with inorganic compounds. They often have characteristic smells and form a very large number of compounds.

Q12. Write a detailed note on classification of organic compounds.
Organic compounds are classified into: (i) open-chain (aliphatic) compounds, such as alkanes and alcohols; (ii) closed-chain (cyclic) compounds, divided into alicyclic compounds (cyclohexane) and aromatic compounds (benzene); and (iii) heterocyclic compounds, whose rings contain nitrogen, oxygen or sulphur (pyridine, furan). They are further classified by functional group into hydrocarbons, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, acids, esters and amines.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single bonds (alkanes); unsaturated hydrocarbons contain a double bond (alkenes, CnH2n) or a triple bond (alkynes, CnH2n-2).
  • Alkanes are called paraffins from Latin parum affinis, meaning little affinity, because they are very unreactive.
  • Alkenes are called olefins oil-forming, because their lower members react with chlorine to form oily liquids.
  • Hydrogenation of alkenes adds hydrogen across the double bond with a nickel catalyst, for example ethene + H2 → ethane, and turns liquid oils into solid ghee.
  • Bromine water test identifies alkenes and alkynes: they decolourize bromine water, while alkanes do not.
  • Ethyne (acetylene) has molecular formula C2H2 and structural formula H-C≡C-H, with a triple bond between the two carbons.
  • Alkanes give substitution reactions because their single bonds cannot take part in addition, for example CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl in sunlight.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Differentiate between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons.
Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single bonds between carbon atoms, so each carbon carries the maximum number of hydrogens, for example alkanes. Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one double or triple bond, so they carry fewer hydrogens, for example alkenes and alkynes, and they undergo addition reactions.

Q2. A compound consisting of four carbon atoms has a triple bond in it. How many hydrogen atoms are present in it?
A four-carbon compound with one triple bond is an alkyne, general formula CnH2n-2. For n = 4, hydrogens = 2(4) - 2 = 6. The compound is butyne (C4H6).

Q3. Why are the alkanes called 'paraffins'?
Alkanes are called paraffins (from Latin parum affinis, meaning 'little affinity') because they are very unreactive. Their single bonds are strong and non-polar, so they do not readily react with acids, bases or oxidizing agents under ordinary conditions.

Q4. What do you know about hydrogenation of alkenes?
Hydrogenation of alkenes is the addition of hydrogen across the double bond in the presence of a nickel catalyst, converting an alkene into an alkane. For example, ethene + H2 → ethane. This reaction is used to convert liquid vegetable oils (unsaturated) into solid ghee (saturated).

Q5. How are alkyl halides reduced?
Alkyl halides are reduced by replacing the halogen atom with hydrogen. For example, methyl chloride reacts with zinc and acid, or with lithium aluminium hydride, to give methane: CH3Cl + [H] → CH4 + HCl. The halogen is removed as a halide ion.

Q6. Why are the alkanes used as fuel?
Alkanes are used as fuel because they burn in air with a clean flame, releasing a large amount of heat energy. Their combustion gives carbon dioxide and water, and fuels such as natural gas (methane), petrol and kerosene are all mixtures of alkanes.

Q7. How can you prepare ethene from alcohol and ethyl bromide?
From alcohol: ethanol is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid at 170 degrees C, which removes water (dehydration) to give ethene: C2H5OH → C2H4 + H2O. From ethyl bromide: ethyl bromide is heated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide, which removes HBr (dehydrohalogenation) to give ethene: C2H5Br + KOH → C2H4 + KBr + H2O.

Q8. Identify propane from propene with a chemical test.
Pass each gas through bromine water: propene (an alkene) decolourizes bromine water because it adds bromine across its double bond, while propane (an alkane) does not change the colour. Propene also decolourizes dilute KMnO4 solution, while propane does not.

Q9. Why are the alkenes called 'olefins'?
Alkenes are called olefins (oil-forming) because their lower members react with chlorine to form oily liquids. For example, ethene reacts with chlorine to give 1,2-dichloroethane, an oily liquid, and this oil-forming property gave the family its old name.

Q10. Why can't alkanes be oxidized with KMnO4 solution?
Alkanes cannot be oxidized by KMnO4 because they have only strong, non-polar single bonds and no double or triple bond for the oxidizing agent to attack. Dilute KMnO4 therefore keeps its purple colour with alkanes, while it is decolourized by alkenes and alkynes.

Q11. What are the addition reactions? Explain with an example.
Addition reactions are reactions in which atoms or groups add across a double or triple bond, breaking the multiple bond and forming a saturated product. For example, ethene reacts with bromine: C2H4 + Br2 → C2H4Br2 (1,2-dibromoethane), where the double bond becomes a single bond and each carbon gains a bromine atom.

Q12. Justify that alkanes give substitution reactions.
Alkanes give substitution reactions because their single bonds cannot take part in addition, so a hydrogen atom is replaced by another atom or group instead. For example, methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl, where a hydrogen is substituted by chlorine. Further substitution gives CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4.

Q13. Both alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons. State the one most significant difference between them.
The most significant difference is the type of multiple bond: alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C) and follow the general formula CnH2n, while alkynes contain a carbon-carbon triple bond (C≡C) and follow CnH2n-2. Alkynes are therefore more unsaturated and more reactive than alkenes.

Q14. Write the molecular, dot and cross and structural formula of ethyne.
Ethyne (acetylene) has molecular formula C2H2. Its structural formula is H-C≡C-H, with a triple bond between the two carbons. In dot-and-cross form, draw the two carbons sharing three pairs of electrons (the triple bond) and each carbon sharing one pair with a hydrogen atom.

Q15. Why are hydrocarbons soluble in organic solvents?
Hydrocarbons are non-polar covalent compounds, and they dissolve in non-polar organic solvents such as benzene, carbon tetrachloride and ether, following the rule 'like dissolves like'. They do not dissolve in water because water is polar and cannot break the weak forces between hydrocarbon molecules.

Q16. Give the physical properties of alkanes.
Alkanes are colourless, odourless (except the lower ones which have a faint smell), non-polar covalent compounds. Their melting and boiling points increase with molecular size. The first four are gases, the next ones up to about C17 are liquids, and higher ones are solids. They are insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents, and less dense than water.

Q17. How can you identify ethane from ethene?
Ethene decolourizes bromine water and dilute KMnO4 solution, while ethane does not. Ethene also burns with a more smoky flame than ethane. The bromine water test is the standard identification: only the unsaturated ethene removes the reddish-brown colour.

Q18. Why does the colour of bromine water discharge on addition of ethene in it?
Ethene adds bromine across its double bond to form colourless 1,2-dibromoethane. The reddish-brown colour of bromine water is due to free bromine, and as bromine is consumed in the addition reaction, the colour disappears.

Q19. State one important use of each: (i) Ethene (ii) Acetylene (iii) Chloroform (iv) Carbon tetrachloride.
(i) Ethene: used to make polythene plastic and to ripen fruits artificially. (ii) Acetylene: used in oxy-acetylene welding and cutting of metals, and to make PVC. (iii) Chloroform: used as a solvent and formerly as an anaesthetic. (iv) Carbon tetrachloride: used as a solvent for fats and oils and in fire extinguishers (now limited because it harms the ozone layer).

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. What type of reactions are given by alkanes? Explain with reference to halogenation of alkanes.
Alkanes mainly give substitution reactions, in which a hydrogen atom is replaced by another atom, and combustion reactions. In halogenation, for example, methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight in stages: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl, then CH3Cl + Cl2 → CH2Cl2 + HCl, and so on to CCl4. Each step substitutes one more hydrogen by chlorine, with sunlight providing the energy to break the chlorine molecule into reactive atoms.

Q2. Alkanes are a source of heat. Explain it.
Alkanes burn in excess oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of heat energy because strong C=O and O-H bonds are formed. For example, CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O + heat. This is why natural gas, petrol, diesel and kerosene, all mixtures of alkanes, are used as fuels for cooking, heating, transport and power generation.

Q3. Prepare the following as directed: (i) ethane from ethene (ii) acetylene from tetrahalide (iii) carbon tetrachloride from methane (iv) ethylene glycol from ethene (v) 1,2-dibromoethane from ethene (vi) glyoxal from acetylene.
(i) Ethane from ethene: hydrogenation with H2 and nickel catalyst, C2H4 + H2 → C2H6. (ii) Acetylene from tetrahalide: 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane reacts with zinc dust (dehalogenation) to give acetylene. (iii) Carbon tetrachloride from methane: chlorination in sunlight through successive substitution to CCl4. (iv) Ethylene glycol from ethene: ethene is oxidized with cold dilute KMnO4 (or via the epoxide) to give ethane-1,2-diol. (v) 1,2-dibromoethane from ethene: addition of bromine, C2H4 + Br2 → C2H4Br2. (vi) Glyoxal from acetylene: acetylene is oxidized (for example with nitric acid or by ozonolysis) to give glyoxal (OHC-CHO).

Q4. Explain the oxidation of acetylene.
Acetylene burns in air with a very hot, smoky flame: 2C2H2 + 5O2 → 4CO2 + 2H2O + heat. With a limited supply of oxygen it gives carbon monoxide and soot. Controlled oxidation with reagents such as KMnO4 or nitric acid breaks the triple bond and gives oxidized products such as glyoxal and then oxalic acid, showing that alkynes are easily oxidized because of their triple bond.

Q5. Write balanced chemical equations for the following reactions. Also, name the products that are formed. (i) A mixture of ethyne and hydrogen is passed over heated nickel (ii) Ethyne is treated with chlorine (iii) Ethyne is burnt in air (iv) Ethyne is passed through bromine water.
(i) C2H2 + 2H2 → C2H6 (ethane). (ii) C2H2 + 2Cl2 → C2H2Cl4 (1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane). (iii) 2C2H2 + 5O2 → 4CO2 + 2H2O (carbon dioxide and water). (iv) C2H2 + 2Br2 → C2H2Br4 (1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane); the bromine water is decolourized.

Q6. Explain briefly: (i) Why butane undergoes substitution reactions? (ii) There are millions of organic compounds. (iii) Acetylene undergoes addition reactions in two stages. (iv) Alkynes are more reactive than alkanes.
(i) Butane is an alkane with only single bonds, so it cannot add across a bond; instead a hydrogen is substituted by another atom, as in chlorination. (ii) There are millions of organic compounds because carbon catenates into chains, branches and rings, forms bonds with many elements, and shows isomerism. (iii) Acetylene has a triple bond, so addition occurs in two stages: first one pi bond breaks to give an alkene, then the second pi bond breaks to give a saturated product. (iv) Alkynes are more reactive than alkanes because their triple bond has two easily broken pi bonds and a high electron density that attracts electrophiles.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Photosynthesis makes carbohydrates in plants: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2 in sunlight and chlorophyll.
