lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. How do plants synthesize carbohydrates?
Plants synthesize carbohydrates by photosynthesis: in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water combine to form glucose and oxygen: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2. The glucose is then converted into starch for storage and into cellulose for cell walls.

Q2. Give the characteristics of monosaccharides.
Monosaccharides are the simplest sugars, with one sugar unit that cannot be hydrolyzed further. They are sweet, soluble in water, crystalline solids, and have the general formula (CH2O)n. Examples are glucose, fructose and galactose, all with formula C6H12O6 but different structures.

Q3. What is the difference between glucose and fructose?
Glucose and fructose are both monosaccharides with formula C6H12O6, but glucose is an aldose (it contains an aldehyde group -CHO) while fructose is a ketose (it contains a ketone group >C=O). Glucose is the main blood sugar and is less sweet, while fructose is the sweetest sugar, found in fruits and honey.

Q4. Give an example of a disaccharide. How is it hydrolyzed into monosaccharides?
Sucrose (table sugar) is a disaccharide made of glucose and fructose. On hydrolysis with dilute acid or the enzyme invertase, it splits into its two monosaccharides: sucrose + water → glucose + fructose. Similarly, maltose hydrolyzes into two glucose molecules and lactose into glucose and galactose.

Q5. Give the characteristics of polysaccharides.
Polysaccharides are large molecules made of many monosaccharide units joined together. They are usually not sweet, are insoluble or only slightly soluble in water, and do not taste sweet. Examples are starch (food storage in plants), glycogen (storage in animals) and cellulose (plant cell walls).

Q6. Where are the proteins found?
Proteins are found in all living cells and in foods such as meat, fish, eggs, milk, cheese, pulses, beans and nuts. In the body they form muscles, skin, hair, nails, enzymes, hormones and antibodies, and they are essential for growth and repair.

Q7. Describe the uses of carbohydrates.
Carbohydrates are the main source of energy for the body, as glucose is oxidized to release energy. They are also used as food (starch, sugar), as structural material (cellulose in plants), in making paper and cloth (cellulose), and as storage food (starch in plants, glycogen in animals).

Q8. Lactose is a disaccharide; which monosaccharides are present in it?
Lactose, the sugar of milk, is made of glucose and galactose joined together. On hydrolysis it splits into one molecule of glucose and one molecule of galactose.

Q9. Why are the ten amino acids essential for us?
Ten amino acids are called essential because the human body cannot make them, so they must be obtained from food. They are needed to build body proteins, enzymes and hormones, and without them growth, repair and normal body functions cannot continue.

Q10. How are proteins formed?
Proteins are formed when amino acids join together by peptide bonds, with the loss of a water molecule between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next. Long chains of amino acids fold into specific shapes to form proteins, and the sequence of amino acids decides the protein's function.

Q11. How is gelatin obtained?
Gelatin is obtained by boiling animal skin, bones and connective tissue in water, which breaks down the protein collagen into gelatin. The solution is then filtered, concentrated and dried into sheets or powder, used in food, capsules and photography.

Q12. Give the general formula of the lipids.
Lipids are fats and oils, formed from fatty acids and glycerol. Their general composition is that of esters of glycerol with long-chain fatty acids; a fat molecule (triglyceride) is formed from one glycerol and three fatty acid molecules, with the loss of three water molecules.

Q13. Name two fatty acids with their formulae.
Two fatty acids are: palmitic acid, C15H31COOH (a saturated fatty acid found in palm oil), and oleic acid, C17H33COOH (an unsaturated fatty acid found in olive oil). Stearic acid, C17H35COOH, is another common example.

Q14. Give the types of vitamins.
Vitamins are divided into two types: fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K), which are stored in body fat and liver, and water-soluble vitamins (B-complex and C), which dissolve in water, are not stored in large amounts, and must be taken regularly in food.

Q15. What is the significance of vitamins?
Vitamins are essential in small amounts for normal growth, health and resistance to disease. They regulate body processes, help enzymes work, protect against deficiency diseases (such as scurvy from lack of vitamin C and rickets from lack of vitamin D), and keep skin, eyes, bones and blood healthy.

Q16. Describe the sources and uses of vitamin A.
Vitamin A is found in fish liver oil, butter, eggs, milk, carrots, mangoes and green leafy vegetables (as carotene). It is needed for good eyesight, healthy skin and mucous membranes, growth, and resistance to infections. Its deficiency causes night blindness and dry skin.

Q17. Justify that water soluble vitamins are not injurious to health.
Water-soluble vitamins (B-complex and C) are not injurious in normal amounts because any excess is dissolved in water and excreted in urine, so they do not build up to toxic levels in the body. Fat-soluble vitamins, by contrast, are stored in fat and can become harmful in excess.

Q18. What do you mean by genetic code of life?
The genetic code of life is the information stored in DNA that decides the characteristics of an organism. It is written in the sequence of four bases (adenine, thymine, guanine, cytosine) along the DNA molecule, and each set of three bases (a codon) specifies one amino acid in a protein, thus controlling heredity.

Q19. What is the function of DNA?
DNA stores and transmits hereditary information from parents to offspring. It carries the instructions for making all the proteins of the body, controls the growth and working of cells, and passes genetic characters from one generation to the next through its base sequence.

Q20. How do you justify that RNA works like a messenger?
RNA works like a messenger because it copies the genetic instructions from DNA in the nucleus and carries them to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm, where proteins are made. This messenger RNA (mRNA) tells the ribosome the exact sequence of amino acids to join, so the correct protein is built.

mcqs.why: Vitamin A is needed for good eyesight, healthy skin, growth and resistance to infection, and its deficiency causes night blindness and dry skin.

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. What are carbohydrates? How are monosaccharides prepared? Give their characteristics.
Carbohydrates are organic compounds of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2:1, first made by plants through photosynthesis. Monosaccharides are prepared by hydrolysis of disaccharides and polysaccharides: for example, starch hydrolyzes to glucose, and sucrose to glucose and fructose. Their characteristics are: they are sweet, soluble in water, crystalline, cannot be hydrolyzed further, and have formula (CH2O)n.

Q2. Explain oligosaccharides.
Oligosaccharides are carbohydrates made of a small number (2 to 10) of monosaccharide units joined by glycosidic bonds. The most important are disaccharides: sucrose (glucose + fructose), maltose (glucose + glucose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). They are sweet, soluble in water, and on hydrolysis they give their constituent monosaccharides.

Q3. What are polysaccharides? Give their properties.
Polysaccharides are large carbohydrates made of hundreds or thousands of monosaccharide units. Their properties are: they are not sweet, they are insoluble or sparingly soluble in water, they do not reduce Fehling's solution, and on complete hydrolysis they give monosaccharides. Examples are starch, glycogen and cellulose, which serve as food storage and structural material.

Q4. Explain the sources and uses of proteins.
Proteins are obtained from animal sources (meat, fish, eggs, milk) and plant sources (pulses, beans, nuts, wheat). Their uses in the body are: building and repairing tissues, forming enzymes that speed up reactions, forming hormones that regulate body functions, forming antibodies that fight disease, and providing energy when carbohydrates and fats are short.

Q5. Explain that amino acids are building blocks of proteins.
Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins because proteins are long chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. There are 20 common amino acids, and the order in which they are joined decides the shape and function of the protein. Just as letters form words, different sequences of amino acids form the thousands of different proteins in living things.

Q6. Explain the sources and uses of lipids.
Lipids come from animal fats (butter, ghee, meat fat) and plant oils (olive oil, sunflower oil, groundnut oil). Their uses are: they are a concentrated source of energy, they insulate the body against heat loss, they protect internal organs, they carry fat-soluble vitamins, and they form cell membranes.

Q7. Give the importance of vitamins.
Vitamins are important because, although needed in tiny amounts, they are essential for health: they prevent deficiency diseases, help the body use carbohydrates, proteins and fats, support growth, eyesight, blood formation and bone formation, and strengthen resistance to infections. A diet lacking any vitamin leads to a specific deficiency disease.

Q8. Describe the sources, uses and deficiency symptoms of water soluble vitamins.
Water-soluble vitamins are the B-complex (B1, B2, B6, B12, niacin, folic acid) and vitamin C. Sources are whole grains, pulses, meat, eggs, milk, citrus fruits and green vegetables. They are used for energy release, blood formation, nerve function and wound healing. Deficiency symptoms are: beri-beri (B1), sore tongue and skin (B2), anaemia (B12, folic acid), pellagra (niacin), and scurvy with bleeding gums (vitamin C).

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Environmental Chemistry I - The Atmosphere

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Troposphere holds about 75% of the atmosphere's mass, and temperature there falls by about 6.5 degrees C per kilometre with height.
  • Primary pollutants are emitted directly, for example CO, SO2 and dust; secondary pollutants, for example ozone and PAN, form in the air from primary pollutants.
  • Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin about 300 times more strongly than oxygen, so it starves the body's tissues of oxygen.
  • Ozone layer forms in the stratosphere when ultraviolet light splits O2 into oxygen atoms and O + O2 → O3.
  • CFCs deplete ozone because ultraviolet light frees chlorine atoms, and each chlorine atom destroys many ozone molecules in a chain reaction.
  • Acid rain is rain with a pH below 5.6, made acidic by dissolved oxides of sulphur and nitrogen.
  • Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas: it lets sunlight in but absorbs the infrared radiation given out by the Earth, trapping heat.

mcqs.q: About what percentage of the atmosphere's mass is held in the troposphere?
mcqs.why: The key facts state the troposphere holds about 75% of the atmosphere's mass, leaving 100 - 75 = 25% in all the higher layers combined.

mcqs.q: Temperature in the troposphere falls by about 6.5 degrees C per kilometre. What is the fall over 2 kilometres?
mcqs.why: Working: fall = 6.5 x 2 = 13 degrees C. The rate of about 6.5 degrees C per kilometre multiplied by 2 kilometres gives a 13 degree fall.

options: Carbon monoxide emitted from a source
mcqs.why: Primary pollutants are emitted directly, for example CO, SO2 and dust; secondary pollutants such as ozone and PAN form in the air from primary pollutants.

mcqs.q: Secondary pollutants such as ozone and PAN are:
options: Formed in the air from primary pollutants
mcqs.why: The notes define secondary pollutants as those formed in the air from primary pollutants, with ozone and PAN given as the examples, unlike directly emitted CO and SO2.

mcqs.q: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin about how many times more strongly than oxygen?
mcqs.why: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin about 300 times more strongly than oxygen, so it starves the body's tissues of oxygen even at low concentrations.

mcqs.q: The ozone layer forms in the stratosphere when ultraviolet light first splits:
mcqs.why: Ultraviolet light splits O2 into oxygen atoms, and then O + O2 -> O3 forms ozone in the stratosphere, as given in the key facts.

mcqs.q: CFCs deplete ozone because ultraviolet light frees which atoms that destroy many ozone molecules in a chain reaction?
mcqs.why: Ultraviolet light frees chlorine atoms from CFCs, and each chlorine atom destroys many ozone molecules in a chain reaction, thinning the ozone layer.

mcqs.q: Acid rain is defined as rain with a pH:
mcqs.why: Acid rain is rain with a pH below 5.6, made acidic by dissolved oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, so it is more acidic than ordinary rain.

mcqs.q: Acid rain is made acidic mainly by dissolved oxides of:
mcqs.why: The key facts state acid rain has pH below 5.6 and is made acidic by dissolved oxides of sulphur and nitrogen from polluted air.

mcqs.q: Carbon dioxide acts as a greenhouse gas because it:
options: Blocks all sunlight from reaching Earth
Lets sunlight in but absorbs infrared radiation given out by the Earth
mcqs.why: CO2 lets sunlight in but absorbs the infrared radiation given out by the Earth, trapping heat in the atmosphere like glass in a greenhouse.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Explain the phenomenon of decreasing temperature in troposphere.
In the troposphere, temperature decreases with height because the air is heated mainly from the Earth's surface, not directly by the Sun. The ground absorbs sunlight and warms the air touching it, and this warm air rises and cools as it expands. The higher air is therefore farther from the heat source and colder, falling by about 6.5 degrees C per kilometre.

Q2. Differentiate between primary and secondary air pollutants.
Primary pollutants are emitted directly into the air from a source, for example carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and dust. Secondary pollutants are not emitted directly but are formed in the air by reactions between primary pollutants, for example ozone and peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) formed by sunlight acting on nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons in photochemical smog.

Q3. State the major sources of CO and CO2 emission.
Major sources of carbon monoxide are incomplete burning of fuels in vehicles, furnaces and cigarette smoke. Major sources of carbon dioxide are complete burning of fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) in power stations, vehicles and factories, respiration of living things, and deforestation, which removes the trees that absorb CO2.

Q4. CO2 is responsible for heating up atmosphere, how?
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas: it allows short-wave sunlight to pass through to the Earth but absorbs the long-wave infrared radiation given out by the warmed Earth, and re-radiates part of it back downwards. This traps heat in the atmosphere, warming it, just as glass traps heat in a greenhouse. Increasing CO2 therefore increases global warming.

Q5. CO is a hidden enemy, explain its action.
Carbon monoxide is a hidden enemy because it is colourless and odourless, so it cannot be seen or smelled, yet it is highly poisonous. It combines with haemoglobin in the blood about 300 times more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen. The body's tissues are starved of oxygen, causing headache, dizziness, unconsciousness and death.

Q6. What threats are there to human health due to SO2 gas as air pollutant?
Sulphur dioxide irritates the eyes, nose, throat and lungs, causing coughing, breathing difficulty and worsening of asthma and bronchitis. Long exposure damages lung tissue and reduces resistance to infections, and it also forms acid rain which harms crops, buildings and water life.

Q7. Which air pollutant is produced on anaerobic decomposition of organic matter?
Methane (CH4) is produced by anaerobic decomposition (decay without oxygen) of organic matter, for example in marshes, paddy fields, landfills and the stomachs of cattle. Hydrogen sulphide, with its rotten-egg smell, is also produced in smaller amounts during anaerobic decay.

Q8. How does acid rain increase the acidity of soil?
Acid rain contains sulphuric and nitric acids formed from SO2 and nitrogen oxides. When it falls on soil, its hydrogen ions replace useful nutrients such as calcium, magnesium and potassium on soil particles, washing them away. It also releases toxic aluminium ions into the soil solution, making the soil more acidic and harmful to plant roots.

Q9. Point out two serious effects of ozone depletion.
Two serious effects of ozone depletion are: (i) more ultraviolet radiation reaches the Earth, increasing skin cancer, eye cataracts and damage to the immune system in humans; (ii) it harms plants, plankton and aquatic life, reducing crop yields and disturbing food chains in the oceans.

Q10. How is ozone layer formed in stratosphere?
In the stratosphere, ultraviolet sunlight splits oxygen molecules (O2) into oxygen atoms. Each free oxygen atom then combines with another oxygen molecule to form ozone (O3): O + O2 → O3. This ozone absorbs further ultraviolet radiation, which both protects life below and warms the stratosphere.

Q11. Why does 75% of the atmospheric mass lie within the troposphere?
About 75% of the atmosphere's mass lies in the troposphere because air is compressible and gravity pulls it downwards, so the lowest layer is the densest. The troposphere is also the layer in contact with the Earth's surface, where most water vapour and dust are present, adding to its mass.

Q12. How is ozone layer being depleted by chlorofluorocarbons?
Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), used in refrigerators and sprays, rise to the stratosphere where ultraviolet light breaks them apart, releasing chlorine atoms. Each chlorine atom destroys many ozone molecules in a chain reaction: Cl + O3 → ClO + O2, then ClO + O → Cl + O2, freeing the chlorine to destroy more ozone. This thins the ozone layer, especially over the poles.

By the ozone layer above it
mcqs.why: The ground absorbs sunlight and warms the air touching it; higher air is farther from this heat source and cools as it expands, falling about 6.5 degrees C per kilometre.

mcqs.why: Major sources of CO are incomplete burning of fuels in vehicles, furnaces and cigarette smoke, whereas complete burning of fossil fuels is a major source of CO2.

options: Re-radiates part of it back downwards
Reflects all sunlight back to space
mcqs.why: CO2 allows short-wave sunlight through but absorbs long-wave infrared given out by the Earth and re-radiates part back downwards, warming the atmosphere.

options: Irritating eyes, nose, throat and lungs and worsening asthma and bronchitis
Causing night blindness and dry skin

mcqs.why: Methane is produced by anaerobic decomposition, decay without oxygen, of organic matter in marshes, paddy fields, landfills and the stomachs of cattle.

options: Aluminium ions into the soil solution
mcqs.why: Hydrogen ions in acid rain wash away calcium, magnesium and potassium from soil particles and release toxic aluminium ions, harming plant roots.

options: Harms plants, plankton and aquatic life and disturbs ocean food chains
Stops photosynthesis completely in all plants
mcqs.why: Ozone depletion lets more UV reach Earth, increasing skin cancer and cataracts in humans and harming plants, plankton and aquatic life, reducing crop yields.

mcqs.q: About 75% of atmospheric mass lies in the troposphere because:
options: Air is compressible and gravity pulls it downwards, so the lowest layer is densest
The troposphere is the thickest layer of all
Ozone is concentrated in the troposphere
Most gases are produced at the Earth's surface only
mcqs.why: Gravity pulls compressible air downwards so the lowest layer is densest; the troposphere also holds most water vapour and dust, adding to its mass.

mcqs.q: In CFC ozone depletion, after Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2, the chlorine atom is freed again by:
mcqs.why: The chain is Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2, then ClO + O -> Cl + O2; the freed chlorine destroys more ozone, so one atom destroys many ozone molecules.

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Write down the significance of atmospheric gases.
Atmospheric gases are significant because: nitrogen (78%) dilutes oxygen and is needed for proteins; oxygen (21%) is needed for respiration and combustion; carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis and keeps the Earth warm; argon is an inert filler; water vapour forms clouds and rain; and ozone in the stratosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation. Together they make life on Earth possible.

Q2. Give the characteristics of troposphere. Why does temperature decrease upwards in this sphere?
The troposphere is the lowest layer, about 12 km thick, containing 75% of the air's mass and almost all water vapour and weather (clouds, rain, storms). Temperature decreases upwards because the air is heated from the ground: the Earth's surface absorbs sunlight and warms the air above it, and air higher up is farther from this heat source and expands and cools as pressure falls.

Q3. What are the characteristics of stratosphere? Why does temperature increase upwards in this sphere?
The stratosphere lies above the troposphere up to about 50 km, is dry and almost free of weather, and contains the ozone layer. Temperature increases upwards in the stratosphere because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, warming the upper part of the layer. The top of the stratosphere is therefore warmer than its bottom.

Q4. CO2 is necessary for plants but why is its increasing concentration alarming for us?
Carbon dioxide is necessary for photosynthesis, but its increasing concentration is alarming because it is a greenhouse gas that traps heat and causes global warming. This leads to melting of glaciers and sea-level rise, changes in rainfall, droughts and floods, damage to crops and ecosystems, and more extreme weather, threatening human life and food supply.

Q5. Why is CO considered a health hazard?
Carbon monoxide is a health hazard because it is colourless and odourless, so it gives no warning, and it binds to haemoglobin about 300 times more strongly than oxygen. Even small amounts reduce the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, causing headache, dizziness, tiredness and confusion, and larger amounts cause unconsciousness and death by suffocation.

Q6. Define acid rain. How is it formed and what are its effects?
Acid rain is rain with a pH below 5.6, made acidic by dissolved oxides of sulphur and nitrogen. It forms when SO2 and NOx from burning fossil fuels react with water and oxygen in the air to give sulphuric and nitric acids, which fall as rain or snow. Its effects are: damage to crops and forests, acidification of soil and lakes killing fish, corrosion of buildings and monuments (especially marble), and irritation of human lungs.

Q7. Compounds of sulphur are air pollutants. Describe the sources of these compounds along with their effects.
Sulphur compounds, mainly sulphur dioxide (SO2) and hydrogen sulphide (H2S), come from burning coal and oil, smelting of sulphide ores, volcanic eruptions, and decay of organic matter. Their effects are: irritation of eyes and lungs, worsening of asthma, formation of acid rain that damages soil, water life and buildings, and haziness (smog) that reduces visibility.

Q8. Where does ozone layer lie in atmosphere? How is it depleting and how can we prevent its depletion?
The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere, about 20 to 30 km above the Earth. It is being depleted by chlorine and bromine released from chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons, which destroy ozone in chain reactions. Its depletion can be prevented by banning CFCs and halons (as under the Montreal Protocol), using safer substitutes in refrigerators and sprays, and reducing the use of chemicals that release chlorine into the atmosphere.

Q9. Oxides of nitrogen cause air pollution. Describe the sources of these compounds.
Oxides of nitrogen (NO and NO2) come mainly from vehicles and power stations, where high temperatures cause nitrogen and oxygen in the air to combine during fuel burning. Other sources are lightning, bacterial action in soil, and the use of nitrogen fertilizers. They cause photochemical smog, acid rain, irritation of lungs, and damage to plants.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Water dissolves polar substances because its polar molecules attract ions and polar molecules by ion-dipole forces and hydrogen bonding.
  • Temporary hardness is caused by calcium and magnesium hydrogen carbonates and is removed by boiling; permanent hardness is caused by their sulphates and chlorides.
  • pH + pOH = 14 and [H+][OH-] = 10^-14, the relations used for every pH and pOH calculation.
  • Waterborne diseases include cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis A and giardiasis, and are prevented by boiled or chlorinated water, proper sewage disposal and hand washing.
  • Sewage treatment runs in stages: screening, sedimentation, biological treatment with bacteria, and disinfection with chlorine.
  • Detergents harm aquatic life because their phosphates cause algal blooms that use up oxygen, and their chemicals are toxic to fish.
  • Water is a universal solvent because its polar molecules dissolve ionic compounds, polar compounds and gases alike.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. How does water rise in plants?
Water rises in plants through the xylem vessels by a combination of forces: root pressure pushes water up from the roots, capillary action pulls it through the narrow vessels, and transpiration pull draws it upwards as water evaporates from the leaves. Cohesion between water molecules keeps the water column continuous.

Q2. Which forces are responsible for dissolving polar substances in water?
Polar substances dissolve in water because of the attraction between their charged or partly charged ends and the polar water molecules. Ion-dipole forces act between ions and water molecules, and hydrogen bonding acts between polar molecules and water. These forces pull the solute particles apart and surround them with water molecules (hydration).

Q3. Why are non-polar compounds insoluble in water?
Non-polar compounds are insoluble in water because water molecules are strongly attracted to each other by hydrogen bonds, and non-polar molecules cannot form such bonds with water. Water therefore prefers to stay bonded to itself rather than to surround the non-polar particles, so the non-polar substance remains separate.

Q4. How does water dissolve sugar and alcohol?
Sugar and alcohol dissolve in water because they contain hydroxyl (-OH) groups that form hydrogen bonds with water molecules. When sugar is added to water, its molecules are pulled apart by water molecules forming hydrogen bonds with them, and the sugar spreads evenly through the water. Alcohol mixes in the same way through its -OH group.

Q5. How does limestone dissolve in water?
Limestone (calcium carbonate) is almost insoluble in pure water, but it dissolves in water containing dissolved carbon dioxide, which forms weak carbonic acid. The acid reacts with calcium carbonate to give soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate: CaCO3 + CO2 + H2O → Ca(HCO3)2. This is how caves and underground water become hard.

Q6. Differentiate between soft and hard water.
Soft water lathers easily with soap and contains very few dissolved calcium and magnesium salts. Hard water does not lather easily with soap, forming a scum instead, because it contains dissolved calcium and magnesium hydrogen carbonates (temporary hardness) or sulphates and chlorides (permanent hardness).

Q7. What are the causes of hardness in water?
Hardness in water is caused by dissolved calcium and magnesium salts picked up as water passes over rocks and soil. Temporary hardness is caused by calcium and magnesium hydrogen carbonates, and permanent hardness by their sulphates and chlorides, which do not break down on boiling.

Q8. What are the effects of temporary hardness in water?
Temporary hardness wastes soap by forming scum, leaves deposits (fur) in kettles, boilers and pipes that waste fuel and can block pipes, makes water taste unpleasant, and makes washing and cooking less effective. It can, however, be removed by boiling, which precipitates the carbonates.

Q9. Mention the disadvantages of detergents.
Disadvantages of detergents are: they do not break down easily (non-biodegradable ones persist in water), they cause foaming in rivers and sewage works, their phosphates cause algal growth (eutrophication) that kills aquatic life, and they can irritate skin and harm water organisms.

Q10. What is the difference between biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances?
Biodegradable substances can be broken down by bacteria and other micro-organisms into harmless substances, for example paper, food waste and soap. Non-biodegradable substances cannot be broken down by micro-organisms and persist in the environment for a long time, for example plastics, many detergents and polythene bags.

Q11. How do detergents make the water unfit for aquatic life?
Detergents make water unfit for aquatic life because their phosphates feed algal blooms that block sunlight and use up oxygen when they decay, suffocating fish. The detergent chemicals themselves are toxic to fish and other organisms, and the foam they form reduces oxygen exchange at the water surface.

Q12. Why are pesticides used?
Pesticides are used to kill pests such as insects, fungi, weeds and rodents that damage crops and spread disease. They protect food production, increase crop yields, and control disease-carrying insects such as mosquitoes, but their overuse pollutes water and harms useful organisms.

Q13. What are the reasons of waterborne diseases?
Waterborne diseases are caused by drinking water contaminated with bacteria, viruses and parasites from human and animal waste, sewage, industrial waste and agricultural runoff. Poor sanitation, broken sewers, flooding and lack of water treatment spread these germs into drinking water supplies.

Q14. How can waterborne diseases be prevented?
Waterborne diseases can be prevented by: treating drinking water by filtration, chlorination or boiling; proper disposal of sewage away from water sources; washing hands and keeping food clean; using clean, covered water storage; and vaccinating against diseases such as cholera and typhoid where available.

lessons.title: Long Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. How does polarity of water molecule play its role to dissolve the substances?
The water molecule is polar because oxygen pulls electrons more strongly than hydrogen, giving oxygen a partial negative charge and hydrogens partial positive charges. This polarity lets water attract ions and polar molecules: the negative oxygen ends surround positive ions and the positive hydrogen ends surround negative ions, pulling solute particles apart and keeping them dissolved. Non-polar substances, which have no charges for water to attract, do not dissolve.

Q2. Explain the methods of removing permanent hardness.
Permanent hardness is removed by: (i) adding washing soda (sodium carbonate), which precipitates calcium and magnesium as insoluble carbonates that can be filtered off; (ii) the ion-exchange (permutit) method, in which hard water passes through a zeolite that exchanges its sodium ions for calcium and magnesium ions; and (iii) distillation, which leaves all dissolved salts behind. Boiling does not remove permanent hardness.

Q3. Explain the water pollution because of industrial waste.
Industrial waste pollutes water when factories discharge chemicals, dyes, heavy metals (lead, mercury, chromium), acids and hot water into rivers without treatment. These poisons kill fish and plants, make water unfit for drinking and irrigation, accumulate in food chains, and hot water reduces dissolved oxygen. Treatment and strict discharge limits are needed to control this pollution.

Q4. Justify the statement: household water is the reason of water pollution.
Household water causes pollution because sewage, detergents, soaps, oils and garbage from homes flow into drains and rivers. Detergent phosphates cause algal blooms, organic waste uses up oxygen as it decays, and germs from sewage spread waterborne diseases. If household wastewater is not treated before discharge, it becomes a major source of water pollution.

Q5. Explain that agricultural effluents are fatal for aquatic life.
Agricultural effluents (fertilizers, pesticides and animal waste washed from fields) are fatal for aquatic life because fertilizers cause algal blooms that block light and consume oxygen, pesticides poison fish, frogs and insects directly, and decaying organic waste further lowers dissolved oxygen. Fish suffocate, food chains collapse, and the water becomes unfit for other life.

Q6. Explain five important waterborne diseases. How can these be prevented?
Five waterborne diseases are: cholera (severe diarrhoea and dehydration), typhoid (fever and weakness), dysentery (bloody diarrhoea), hepatitis A (liver infection and jaundice), and giardiasis (stomach cramps and diarrhoea). They are prevented by drinking boiled or chlorinated water, proper sewage disposal, hand washing, clean food handling, and vaccination against cholera and typhoid.

Q7. Give some disadvantages of hard water.
Disadvantages of hard water are: it wastes soap by forming scum, it forms scale in kettles, boilers and pipes that wastes fuel and blocks flow, it makes clothes stiff and dull after washing, it leaves spots on dishes and glass, and it can cause dryness of skin and hair. It is, however, not harmful to health in normal amounts.

Q8. What is water pollution? Describe the effects of using polluted water.
Water pollution is the contamination of water by harmful substances that make it unfit for its intended use. Effects of using polluted water are: waterborne diseases such as cholera, typhoid and dysentery; poisoning by heavy metals and chemicals; skin and stomach problems; death of fish and aquatic plants; damage to crops when used for irrigation; and foul taste and smell that make water unusable.

Q9. Explain the reasons, why water is considered a universal solvent.
Water is called a universal solvent because its polar molecules can dissolve a very large number of substances: ionic compounds (salts) by ion-dipole attraction, polar compounds (sugar, alcohol) by hydrogen bonding, and gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide. Almost no other common liquid dissolves so many different substances, which is why water carries dissolved minerals, nutrients and wastes in nature and in living bodies.

Q10. Write a note on the treatment of sewage water.
Sewage treatment is carried out in stages: screening removes large objects; sedimentation settles out solids; biological treatment uses bacteria to break down organic matter in aeration tanks; and disinfection with chlorine kills germs. The treated water is then safe to release into rivers, and the sludge is dried and used as manure or disposed of safely.

mcqs.why: Oxygen pulls electrons more strongly than hydrogen, giving oxygen a partial negative charge and the hydrogens partial positive charges, which lets water attract ions and polar molecules.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Froth flotation uses pine oil as a frothing agent: ore particles rise with the froth while gangue sinks.
  • Solvay's process works because sodium hydrogen carbonate is much less soluble in cold water than the other salts, so it precipitates out.
  • Ammonia is recovered in Solvay's process by treating ammonium chloride with slaked lime: 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 → CaCl2 + 2NH3 + 2H2O.
  • Ammonia for urea is made by Haber's process at about 200 atm and 450 degrees C with an iron catalyst: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.
  • Roasting heats a sulphide ore strongly in excess air below its melting point, for example 2ZnS + 3O2 → 2ZnO + 2SO2.
  • Fractional distillation of petroleum heats crude oil to about 400 degrees C and separates it by boiling point into gas, petrol, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen.
  • Urea is made from ammonia and carbon dioxide: 2NH3 + CO2 → NH2CONH2 + H2O.

Both ore and gangue rise together with the froth
mcqs.why: Froth flotation uses pine oil as a frothing agent: ore particles rise with the froth while gangue sinks, so the ore is separated and concentrated.

options: Because sodium chloride is the least soluble salt in cold water

mcqs.why: Solvay's process works because sodium hydrogen carbonate is much less soluble in cold water than the other salts in the mixture, so it precipitates out and can be collected.

mcqs.why: Ammonia is recovered by 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCl2 + 2NH3 + 2H2O; the H count balances (10 on each side, verified), and the ammonia is reused in the process.

mcqs.why: Fractional distillation of petroleum heats crude oil to about 400 degrees C and separates it by boiling point into gas, petrol, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q1. What role is played by pine oil in the froth flotation process?
In froth flotation, pine oil acts as a frothing agent: it is added to the powdered ore mixed with water, and when air is blown through, it helps to form a stable froth on the surface. The ore particles stick to the froth bubbles and rise to the top, while the useless rock (gangue) sinks, so the ore is separated and concentrated.

Q2. Name the various metallurgical operations.
The various metallurgical operations are: concentration of the ore (removal of gangue), roasting or calcination (heating to convert ore to oxide), smelting (reduction of the oxide with carbon or another reducing agent), and refining (purification of the metal, for example by electrolysis or bessemerization).

Q3. How is roasting carried out?
Roasting is carried out by heating a sulphide ore strongly in the presence of excess air, below its melting point. The sulphur is removed as sulphur dioxide gas and the ore is converted into its oxide, for example: 2ZnS + 3O2 → 2ZnO + 2SO2. The oxide is then easier to reduce to the metal.

Q4. Explain process of electrorefining.
In electrorefining, the impure metal is made the anode and a thin strip of pure metal the cathode, in a solution of a salt of that metal. When current passes, the anode dissolves and pure metal deposits on the cathode, while impurities either fall as anode mud or remain in solution. Copper is refined this way using copper sulphate solution.

Q5. What are the advantages of Solvay's process?
Advantages of Solvay's process for making washing soda are: the raw materials (common salt, limestone and ammonia) are cheap and abundant; ammonia is recovered and reused; the process gives a pure product; and it operates continuously on a large scale, making it economical for industry.

Q6. What is the principle of Solvay's process?
The principle of Solvay's process is that sodium hydrogen carbonate is much less soluble in cold water than other salts in the mixture, so it precipitates out. Ammoniacal brine (salt solution saturated with ammonia) is carbonated with CO2, giving NH4HCO3, which reacts with NaCl to precipitate NaHCO3, leaving ammonium chloride in solution. Heating NaHCO3 gives washing soda.

Q7. What happens when ammonical brine is carbonated?
When ammoniacal brine (sodium chloride solution saturated with ammonia) is carbonated, carbon dioxide reacts with ammonia and water to form ammonium hydrogen carbonate, which then reacts with sodium chloride to give sodium hydrogen carbonate as a precipitate and ammonium chloride in solution: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O → NaHCO3 + NH4Cl.

Q8. How is NaHCO3 converted to Na2CO3?
Sodium hydrogen carbonate is converted to sodium carbonate by heating (calcination): 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O. The carbon dioxide released is reused in the carbonation tower, and the sodium carbonate obtained is washing soda.

Q9. How is ammonia recovered in the Solvay's process?
Ammonia is recovered by treating the ammonium chloride left in solution with slaked lime (calcium hydroxide): 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 → CaCl2 + 2NH3 + 2H2O. The ammonia gas released is collected and sent back to saturate fresh brine, so very little ammonia is consumed overall.

Q10. How is ammonia prepared for the synthesis of urea?
Ammonia for urea synthesis is prepared by Haber's process: nitrogen and hydrogen react at high pressure (about 200 atm) and temperature (about 450 degrees C) in the presence of an iron catalyst: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. The ammonia is then reacted with carbon dioxide to make urea: 2NH3 + CO2 → NH2CONH2 + H2O.

Q11. Describe the formation of petroleum.
Petroleum formed millions of years ago from the remains of tiny sea plants and animals buried under layers of sand and mud. Under high pressure and temperature, and without air, the organic matter slowly changed into a dark, viscous liquid mixture of hydrocarbons, trapped in porous rocks beneath impermeable layers.

Q12. What is refining of petroleum and how is it carried out?
Refining of petroleum is the separation of crude oil into useful fractions by fractional distillation. Crude oil is heated to vapour in a furnace and passed into a tall fractionating tower, where vapours cool and condense at different heights according to their boiling points: gases at the top, then petrol, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen at the bottom.

Q13. Give a use of kerosene oil.
Kerosene oil is used as a fuel for lamps and stoves in homes, as fuel for jet aircraft (aviation turbine fuel), and as a solvent for paints and insecticides.

Q14. Describe the difference between diesel oil and fuel oil.
Diesel oil is a lighter fraction (boiling range about 250-350 degrees C) used as fuel in diesel engines of trucks, buses and tractors. Fuel oil is a heavier, thicker fraction (boiling above 350 degrees C) used as fuel in furnaces, ships and power stations, and it needs preheating before it can flow and burn.

Q15. Write down the names of four fractions obtained by the fractional distillation of residual oil.
Four fractions obtained from residual oil are: lubricating oil (used for machinery), paraffin wax (used for candles and polishes), bitumen/asphalt (used for road surfacing), and petroleum coke (used as fuel and in electrodes).

Q16. What is the difference between crude oil and residual oil?
Crude oil is the raw, unrefined mixture of hydrocarbons pumped from the ground, containing fractions from gases to heavy residues. Residual oil is what remains after the lighter fractions (petrol, kerosene, diesel) have been distilled off from crude oil; it is thick, dark and contains the heaviest hydrocarbons, used for fuel oil, lubricating oil and bitumen.

Q17. Which petroleum fraction is used in dry cleaning?
Petrol (gasoline) and the light solvent fraction known as petroleum ether / white spirit are used in dry cleaning, because they dissolve grease and dirt from clothes without using water. Carbon tetrachloride was also used, but it is now avoided because of its harmful effects.

mcqs.q: What role is played by pine oil in the froth flotation process?
options: It acts as a frothing agent that helps form a stable froth so ore particles rise with the bubbles
It dissolves the gangue completely in water
It acts as a reducing agent for the ore
It heats the powdered ore during separation
mcqs.why: Pine oil acts as a frothing agent: when air is blown through powdered ore in water it forms a stable froth, ore particles stick to the bubbles and rise, while gangue sinks.

mcqs.q: Which list gives metallurgical operations in the order described in the notes?
options: Concentration of ore, roasting or calcination, smelting, refining
Electrolysis only, with no other operation
mcqs.why: The metallurgical operations are concentration of the ore (removal of gangue), roasting or calcination, smelting (reduction of the oxide), and refining (purification of the metal).

mcqs.q: In electrorefining, where is the impure metal placed and where does pure metal collect?
options: Impure metal is the cathode and pure metal collects at the anode
Both electrodes are made of pure metal only
Impure metal is the anode and pure metal deposits on the cathode
Impure metal is dissolved without using any electrodes
mcqs.why: In electrorefining the impure metal is the anode and a thin strip of pure metal is the cathode; the anode dissolves and pure metal deposits on the cathode, as with copper.

mcqs.q: Which is an advantage of Solvay's process?
options: It uses very expensive and rare raw materials
Ammonia is thrown away after a single use
It works only on a very small laboratory scale
Raw materials are cheap and abundant, ammonia is recovered and reused, and the product is pure
mcqs.why: Advantages of Solvay's process are cheap and abundant raw materials (salt, limestone, ammonia), recovery and reuse of ammonia, a pure product, and continuous large-scale operation.

mcqs.q: What happens when ammoniacal brine is carbonated in Solvay's process?
options: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl, with NaHCO3 as a precipitate
NaCl is converted directly into Na2CO3 gas
Ammonium chloride precipitates and NaHCO3 stays in solution
Only calcium carbonate is formed as the main product
mcqs.why: Carbonation forms ammonium hydrogen carbonate which reacts with NaCl as NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl, precipitating sodium hydrogen carbonate.

mcqs.q: How is NaHCO3 converted to Na2CO3 in Solvay's process?
options: By dissolving it in cold water and filtering it
By heating it: 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O
By treating it with ammonium chloride solution
By passing electric current through its solution
mcqs.why: Sodium hydrogen carbonate is converted by heating (calcination): 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O; the oxygen balance verifies (6 O atoms on each side) and the CO2 is reused.

mcqs.q: Ammonia for the synthesis of urea is prepared by which process and conditions?
options: Solvay's process at ordinary pressure and temperature
Froth flotation at about 400 degrees C
Haber's process at about 200 atm and 450 degrees C with an iron catalyst
Roasting of ammonium salts in excess air
mcqs.why: Ammonia for urea is prepared by Haber's process: N2 + 3H2 gives 2NH3 at about 200 atm and 450 degrees C with an iron catalyst, then it reacts with CO2 to make urea.

mcqs.q: How was petroleum formed, according to the notes?
options: From dead land plants buried in coal mines
From volcanic lava cooling under the sea
From sand and mud reacting with sea water
From remains of tiny sea plants and animals buried under sand and mud, changed by pressure and heat without air
mcqs.why: Petroleum formed millions of years ago from remains of tiny sea plants and animals buried under sand and mud, changed by high pressure and temperature without air into hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: What is the boiling range of diesel oil, and how does fuel oil differ?
options: Diesel boils at about 250-350 degrees C; fuel oil is heavier and boils above 350 degrees C
Diesel boils at about 40-180 degrees C; fuel oil boils below 40 degrees C
Both diesel and fuel oil boil at exactly 400 degrees C
Diesel boils above 350 degrees C; fuel oil boils at 250-350 degrees C
mcqs.why: Diesel oil is a lighter fraction boiling at about 250-350 degrees C for diesel engines, while fuel oil is heavier, boils above 350 degrees C, and is used in furnaces, ships and power stations.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a fraction obtained from residual oil?
mcqs.why: Fractions obtained from residual oil include lubricating oil for machinery, paraffin wax, bitumen/asphalt for roads, and petroleum coke, so lubricating oil is the residual-oil fraction listed.

lessons.notes_html:
Q1. Describe in detail the various processes involved in the concentration of ore. Explain your answer with the help of diagrams.
Concentration of ore (dressing) removes gangue by physical methods: (i) gravity separation, in which the heavier ore settles faster than gangue in water; (ii) magnetic separation, in which a magnetic ore is pulled away from non-magnetic gangue by a magnet; (iii) froth flotation, in which powdered ore with water and pine oil is agitated with air, so ore particles rise with the froth while gangue sinks; and (iv) leaching, in which the ore is dissolved in a suitable chemical and recovered from solution. Diagrams show the settling tank, magnetic roller and flotation tank for each method.

Q2. Explain the process of roasting with reference to copper.
Roasting of copper ore (copper pyrites, CuFeS2) is heating the concentrated ore strongly in excess air. The sulphur is oxidized to sulphur dioxide and the iron and copper sulphides change into oxides and sulphates, giving a mixture of Cu2S and FeO. The iron oxide is then removed as slag with silica in smelting, leaving copper matte, which is further processed to blister copper.

Q3. Write a detailed note on Ammonia Solvay's process.
The Ammonia-Solvay process makes washing soda (Na2CO3) from common salt, limestone and ammonia. Brine is saturated with ammonia, then carbonated with CO2 from heated limestone to precipitate sodium hydrogen carbonate, which is filtered and heated to give washing soda. Ammonia is recovered from ammonium chloride with slaked lime and reused, and calcium chloride is the main by-product. The process is continuous, cheap and gives pure washing soda.

Q4. Write a note on fractional distillation of petroleum.
Fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions by boiling point. Crude oil is heated to about 400 degrees C, vaporized, and passed into a fractionating tower with trays at decreasing temperatures upwards. Fractions condense at the level matching their boiling range: refinery gas at the top, then petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, lubricating oil and wax, with bitumen remaining at the bottom. Each fraction is then further treated for use.

Q5. How is urea manufactured? Explain showing the flow sheet diagram.
Urea is manufactured by reacting ammonia with carbon dioxide under high pressure (about 200 atm) and temperature (about 190 degrees C): 2NH3 + CO2 → NH2COONH4 (ammonium carbamate), which then loses water to give urea: NH2COONH4 → NH2CONH2 + H2O. The flow sheet shows: ammonia and CO2 fed into a reactor, the product mixture passed to a separator where unreacted gases are recycled, and the urea solution concentrated, crystallized and granulated for use as fertilizer.

Q6. How is crude oil refined? Explain two important fractions of petroleum along with their usage.
Crude oil is refined by fractional distillation in a fractionating tower after heating to vapour, separating it by boiling point into fractions that are then purified. Two important fractions are: petrol (boiling range about 40-180 degrees C), used as fuel for cars and as a solvent; and diesel oil (about 250-350 degrees C), used as fuel for diesel engines in trucks, buses, tractors and generators.

Q7. Write a note in detail on smelting and bessemerization, giving a specific example.
Smelting is heating a roasted or calcined ore with a reducing agent (usually coke) and a flux in a furnace, so the metal oxide is reduced to molten metal and impurities form a slag that floats off. For example, in iron smelting, Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2 in a blast furnace, with limestone flux removing silica as slag. Bessemerization is blowing hot air through molten metal (as in copper matte) to oxidize impurities: for copper, air oxidizes iron sulphide to iron oxide (removed as slag) and then copper sulphide to blister copper, giving a purer metal.

mcqs.q: In gravity separation for concentration of ore, separation is based on what?
options: The heavier ore settles faster than gangue in water
The magnetic ore is pulled away by a magnet
Ore particles rise with froth while gangue sinks
The ore is dissolved in a suitable chemical
mcqs.why: Gravity separation concentrates ore because the heavier ore settles faster than gangue in water; it is one of the physical dressing methods described with diagrams in the notes.

mcqs.q: How does magnetic separation concentrate an ore?
options: By heating the ore strongly in excess air
By pulling a magnetic ore away from non-magnetic gangue with a magnet
By blowing air through ore mixed with pine oil
By reducing the oxide with carbon in a furnace
mcqs.why: In magnetic separation a magnetic ore is pulled away from non-magnetic gangue by a magnet, one of the four concentration methods: gravity, magnetic, froth flotation and leaching.

mcqs.q: What is leaching in the concentration of ore?
options: Heating the ore below its melting point in air
Depositing pure metal on a cathode by electrolysis
Dissolving the ore in a suitable chemical and recovering it from the solution
Blowing hot air through molten metal to oxidize impurities
mcqs.why: Leaching concentrates an ore by dissolving it in a suitable chemical and recovering it from solution, alongside gravity separation, magnetic separation and froth flotation.

mcqs.q: Roasting of copper pyrites (CuFeS2) in excess air mainly does what?
options: It converts the ore directly into pure copper metal
It dissolves copper in water for electrolysis
It removes all iron as a gas at this stage
It oxidizes sulphur to sulphur dioxide and changes the sulphides towards oxides, giving Cu2S and FeO
mcqs.why: Roasting copper pyrites in excess air oxidizes sulphur to SO2 and gives a mixture of Cu2S and FeO; iron oxide is later removed as slag in smelting, leaving copper matte.

mcqs.q: In the detailed Ammonia-Solvay process, what is the main by-product?
mcqs.why: In the Solvay process ammonia is recovered from ammonium chloride with slaked lime and reused, and calcium chloride is the main by-product of the process.

mcqs.q: In fractional distillation of petroleum, which fraction remains at the bottom of the tower?
mcqs.why: Fractions condense at levels matching their boiling range: refinery gas at the top, then petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, lubricating oil and wax, with bitumen remaining at the bottom.

mcqs.q: Under what conditions are ammonia and carbon dioxide reacted to manufacture urea?
options: About 200 atm and about 190 degrees C
mcqs.why: Urea is manufactured by reacting ammonia with carbon dioxide under high pressure (about 200 atm) and temperature (about 190 degrees C), as shown in the flow sheet description.

mcqs.q: What intermediate is formed first when urea is manufactured?
options: Ammonium carbamate, NH2COONH4, which then loses water to give urea
mcqs.why: First 2NH3 + CO2 -> NH2COONH4 (ammonium carbamate), which then loses water: NH2COONH4 -> NH2CONH2 + H2O, giving urea for concentration and granulation.

mcqs.q: What happens during smelting, with iron as the example?
options: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 in a blast furnace, with limestone flux removing silica as slag
Iron ore is dissolved in water and filtered to get iron
Molten iron is refined only by froth flotation
Iron oxide is heated without any reducing agent or flux
mcqs.why: Smelting heats ore with a reducing agent (usually coke) and a flux; for iron, Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 in a blast furnace, and limestone removes silica as slag that floats off.

mcqs.q: What is bessemerization, as described for copper matte?
options: Cooling molten metal slowly in moulds to purify it
Blowing hot air through molten metal to oxidize impurities, giving blister copper
Passing molten metal through a zeolite exchanger
Heating metal with pine oil to form a froth
mcqs.why: Bessemerization blows hot air through molten metal to oxidize impurities: for copper, iron sulphide is oxidized and removed as slag, then copper sulphide gives blister copper, a purer metal.
